protocol_steps.action: Define P and Q regions and the targeting strategy with the author.
protocol_steps.variables_and_units: Atlas coordinates (millimeters from bregma, required author input); viral strategy; projection-specific versus soma-targeted inhibition.
protocol_steps.acceptance_or_stop_rule: Do not begin behavioral testing until the strategy is prespecified and its specificity limits are documented.

protocol_steps.action: Verify opsin expression and anatomical targeting.
protocol_steps.variables_and_units: Percent of opsin-positive P somata that are retrogradely labeled from Q; off-target labeling (counts).
protocol_steps.control: Contralateral or non-targeted hemisphere comparison where appropriate.
protocol_steps.acceptance_or_stop_rule: Proceed only if prespecified overlap and off-target thresholds are met; otherwise retarget.

protocol_steps.action: Verify physiological suppression under the light protocol.
protocol_steps.variables_and_units: Neural firing rate change (percent); light power (milliwatts per square millimeter); pulse frequency (hertz).
protocol_steps.acceptance_or_stop_rule: Proceed only if suppression is reliable and reversible; stop and recalibrate if not.

protocol_steps.action: Calibrate light power to the minimum effective level.
protocol_steps.variables_and_units: Power at fiber tip (milliwatts); duty cycle (percent); tissue temperature change (degrees Celsius).
protocol_steps.control: Matched light in opsin-negative animals; sham fiber placement.
protocol_steps.acceptance_or_stop_rule: Use the lowest power with reliable suppression and no measurable heating or damage; report the calibration curve.
protocol_steps.provenance: proposed; exact power and wavelength are required author inputs

protocol_steps.action: Test whether the animal can detect the light.
protocol_steps.variables_and_units: Performance in a light-cued task (proportion correct); light-only trial responses (proportion).
protocol_steps.acceptance_or_stop_rule: If light is detectable, mitigate by shielding or wavelength choice and keep light-only trials in the analysis.

protocol_steps.action: Habituate animals and train to a prespecified criterion.
protocol_steps.variables_and_units: Sessions to criterion (count); accuracy (proportion correct); trial-initiation latency (milliseconds).
protocol_steps.acceptance_or_stop_rule: Enter test sessions only when accuracy is stable within the prespecified band.

protocol_steps.action: Define and time the retrieval window per trial.
protocol_steps.variables_and_units: Cue onset to choice initiation (milliseconds); light onset and offset timestamps.
protocol_steps.control: No-light interleaved trials in the same session.
protocol_steps.acceptance_or_stop_rule: Discard sessions with mistimed light delivery beyond the prespecified tolerance.

protocol_steps.action: Randomize and blind light and no-light trials within session.
protocol_steps.variables_and_units: Trial counts per condition (count); randomized sequence; counterbalanced side and reward mapping.
protocol_steps.control: Opsin-negative lit animals; coder blinded to condition.
protocol_steps.acceptance_or_stop_rule: Stop if blinding is broken or if light is confounded with side or trial position.

protocol_steps.action: Calibrate sample size from pilot animal-level variance.
protocol_steps.variables_and_units: Variance of animal-level accuracy difference; target power 0.80; alpha 0.05; animals required (count).
protocol_steps.control: Pilot animals not reused in the main analysis.
protocol_steps.acceptance_or_stop_rule: If the required number of animals is infeasible, reduce the number of conditions and report the limitation.
protocol_steps.provenance: proposed; no numeric sample size is asserted here

protocol_steps.action: Run test sessions and collect primary and confound measures.
protocol_steps.variables_and_units: Accuracy (proportion correct); reaction time (milliseconds); speed and distance (centimeters per second, meters); cue detection and reward consumption (proportions).
protocol_steps.control: Interleaved no-light trials; opsin-negative lit controls.
protocol_steps.acceptance_or_stop_rule: Pause the session if animals show distress, seizures or persistent trial-initiation failure.

protocol_steps.action: Analyze with animal-level mixed models and planned contrasts.
protocol_steps.variables_and_units: Log-odds of correct response; fixed effect of light condition; animal random intercepts; effect sizes with confidence intervals.
protocol_steps.control: Prespecified contrast and analysis plan; blinded outcome coding.
protocol_steps.acceptance_or_stop_rule: Report a retrieval-specific effect only if accuracy falls without comparable falls in movement, cue detection or reward consumption.

protocol_steps.action: Apply decision and troubleshooting rules.
protocol_steps.variables_and_units: Suppression efficacy (percent); expression and targeting metrics; behavioral effect sizes.
protocol_steps.acceptance_or_stop_rule: No effect with unverified suppression is inconclusive; a deficit with reduced movement requires redesign or explicit mediation analysis; a selective deficit supports necessity only under tested conditions.

limitations: Only necessity under the tested retrieval window can be addressed; sufficiency and memory-storage claims require different designs.
P has a collateral projection, so projection-specific targeting is the central and fragile assumption of the whole design.
Terminal inhibition and soma inhibition each carry distinct confounds, and neither cleanly isolates synaptic transmission from local circuit effects.
Light power, wavelength, opsin choice, coordinates, task timing and sample size are unknown and require author input or calibration.
Locomotion and cue detection can never be perfectly matched, so an affect-free or motor-free interpretation should not be claimed.
No human expert review of this draft has occurred.

neu-r01.reference_answer:
The valuable biological question is whether the neural representation of a neutral context can become associated with an aversive event when that representation is activated internally, without the animal physically occupying that context during learning. The packet shows that stimulating a previously tagged population can influence retrieval-related behavior. It does not establish that the same intervention can supply a cue during acquisition of a new association. The proposal therefore changes the causal question from whether an existing representation can drive behavior to whether its timed reactivation can contribute to learning. These are different claims and require different experimental phases.

The principal hypothesis is that the tagged contextual ensemble can function as an internal conditioned cue. A competing hypothesis is that activation merely produces generalized arousal, immobility, or an acute aversive state. Another is that the tagging procedure captures cells responsive to common handling or stress rather than context identity. A fourth is that the intervention changes later exploration without forming an association. The design must distinguish these possibilities instead of treating any increase in freezing as confirmation. The anticipated result is conditional: it would be informative only if the controls below remain intact.

Stage one is to create a preregistered timeline with separate labeling, association, retention, and testing periods. Before collecting experimental data, specify which event occurs in each context, when labeling can occur, and when optical stimulation is permitted. Context A is initially neutral; context B is distinguishable and contains the conditioning event; context C is a specificity control. Context identities should be counterbalanced across apparatus so that one odor, floor, room, or experimenter is not confounded with the conceptual role of A. Record cleaning procedures and handling histories consistently.

Stage two is to validate population targeting independently of the behavioral endpoint. Confirm the identity of the activity-dependent labeling construct and the anatomical boundaries of the intended dentate-gyrus population. Use histology and a prespecified anatomical inclusion rule to quantify expression, misplaced expression, and the fraction of tagged cells. Confirm that the labeling window closes before conditioning in B. A separate validation cohort can establish whether the stimulation drives the targeted cells with the intended temporal fidelity. Validation should not select only animals showing the desired memory behavior.

Stage three is to calibrate the intervention. Record the optical device, measured output at the relevant connection, stability over the session, and a justified estimate or measurement of exposure at the target. Validate that the selected pattern produces reliable neural activation without broad movement suppression, obvious tissue damage, or excessive heating. The exact numerical settings, targeting coordinates, and tagging schedule are not established by the packet and must be obtained from verified protocols and local validation before execution. They must not be invented and attributed to the historical paper. Use one frozen parameter set in the confirmatory experiment.

Stage four assigns animals to conditions using concealed random allocation balanced for prespecified factors such as sex, cohort, and baseline locomotion. The central group receives ensemble reactivation during the conditioning event in B after neutral tagging in A. Comparison groups include the same temporal sequence without functional optical activation, activation of the tagged ensemble without the conditioning event, and both events delivered with an explicitly unpaired schedule. Include a labeling control that cannot express the active opsin. These controls address intervention hardware, tagging, associative contingency, and the conditioning event separately.

Stage five performs acquisition while retaining a complete event log. Record the exact timing of context entry, optical commands, behavioral stimuli, and exits on a shared clock. Verify that actual optical output follows the command rather than assuming that a software timestamp proves delivery. Keep the observer and subsequent video scorer unaware of group identity where feasible. Avoid using behavior during this phase as the main evidence for the new association because immediate stimulation could alter movement. All departures from the planned sequence should enter a deviation log before group codes are revealed.

Stage six tests retention in A without optical stimulation and without the conditioning event. Also test a distinct neutral context, with order counterbalanced or with separate cohorts if repeated testing changes the memory. Prespecify whether testing in B is primary, secondary, or part of a separate cohort, because exposing the animal to B can itself alter subsequent behavior. The crucial comparison concerns the interaction between training contingency and test-context identity. A generalized increase across every context would support arousal or generalization more readily than a selective association involving the original representation.

Stage seven defines the behavioral measurement before inspecting condition means. Use a validated movement-based freezing classifier with a documented sampling rate, smoothing rule, minimum episode duration, and treatment of missing frames. Manually audit a blinded subset of videos spanning the full range of movement rather than only extreme examples. Record total movement, exploration, and overt motor capability as complementary outcomes. If possible, include a behaviorally distinct fear-related response in a separate confirmation experiment. Agreement between outcomes is stronger than relying on a single immobility threshold.

Stage eight specifies replication and analysis. The experimental unit for the central claim is the animal, not a video frame, tagged cell, or stimulation pulse. Multiple contexts or time windows within an animal are repeated observations. Estimate group contrasts and the contingency-by-context interaction with uncertainty, while accounting for cohort and repeated measures. Determine sample size from a prespecified smallest meaningful effect and variance information independent of the confirmatory outcomes. Report every assigned animal, loss, technical failure, and anatomical exclusion, with exclusion decisions made without seeing the primary behavioral result.

Stage nine tests mechanism more directly without confusing supportive evidence with necessity. A separate acquisition-specific disruption can ask whether activity in the labeled ensemble is required during the proposed association window. A separate retrieval-specific disruption can test later expression. These manipulations must have their own targeting and efficacy controls. They should not be combined into one uninterpretable permanent lesion. A selective effect on one phase could clarify the role of the ensemble, whereas a global behavioral deficit would not. Network measurements may identify candidate downstream regions but cannot establish synaptic routes merely from simultaneous activation.

The decision rule requires a coherent pattern: the contingent group must show a stronger response in A than the unpaired and inactive-intervention groups, while preserving general movement and showing meaningful discrimination from C. A result appearing only during illumination fails the acquisition claim. Equal responding in A and C leaves generalized fear unresolved. Failed targeting or absent physiological activation makes a negative behavioral result technically ambiguous. Conversely, successful targeting with an adequately precise null result constrains the proposed role under the tested conditions without proving that every possible pattern of activation would fail.

The supported conclusion would concern a learned association involving an experimentally activated contextual representation. It would not establish conscious experience, verbal report, the phenomenology of human false autobiographical memory, or a unique necessary circuit for all contextual learning. Other circuits may mediate expression, and activity-dependent labeling samples a population rather than identifying every relevant neuron. The reference answer is a proposed operational design with explicitly identified missing parameters. Its historical-direction score depends on the causal question, intervention timing, context-specific test, and discriminating prediction, not on naming a later paper or repeating its title.

A useful extension addresses ensemble overlap as a measured confound. Quantify how much the A-tagged population overlaps with activity elicited by B or C in a separately allocated validation cohort. High overlap would weaken the assumption that stimulation supplies a distinctive contextual cue. Keep image-registration methods and positivity thresholds fixed, and summarize overlap at the animal level. This measurement does not replace the contingency test; it evaluates an assumption on which that test depends. If overlap varies with targeting or handling, use that information to improve the next preregistered cohort rather than retrospectively excluding inconvenient animals.

neu-p01.reference_answer: Source identity and the evidential force of the notice are separate questions. On identity, the teaching archive certifies article record NS-12 by R. Vale, 'Projection P in learning', 2023, and the submitted citation matches every field. The source therefore matches an existing record within the supplied archive; it is not a nonexistent article and it is not a fabricated citation. The archive is authoritative only inside this teaching dossier, which bounds how far that verification extends. A retraction notice is also attached. The notice states that animal identities could not be reconciled across acquisition files. That is a specific reliability concern, and it is the reason the record is classed as retracted. The notice does not determine the truth of every biological claim in the paper, does not supply corrected group identities, and does not establish intent or misconduct. Reporting the notice means reporting exactly what it says, with its limits, rather than converting it into a global verdict about the projection. On the evidence, E1 reports lower learned performance after projection inhibition. E2 states that the allocation file and the raw animal identities needed to verify independent groups are unavailable. Together these mean the reported effect cannot be audited: without reliable animal assignment, independence of observations and the composition of the compared groups cannot be checked, so the reported sample size, degrees of freedom and uncertainty cannot be trusted from the summary alone. A small p-value cannot repair a missing allocation record, because the p-value is computed under assumptions about independence and group structure that the missing record is supposed to support. The correct inferential position is that the dossier provides insufficient evidence for the necessity claim, and that this insufficiency does not prove the biological claim false. Absence of trustworthy support is not affirmative evidence of no effect. Incorrect alternatives include saying that the retraction proves the projection has no biological role; that a retracted paper never existed; that the notice supplies corrected group identities; and that a significant summary statistic can substitute for auditable group assignment. Each of these overreads the available material. Discriminating next steps, proposed rather than performed, begin with recovering auditable identity and allocation records if they still exist, and with an independent, preregistered, blinded replication in which animals are the independent unit, groups are balanced and counterbalanced for order, the perturbation is validated for expression, anatomical spread and physiological suppression, and opsin-negative lit controls plus no-light trials are included. A necessity design should inhibit only during acquisition or only during retrieval according to the prespecified question, and should measure locomotion and cue detection so that a performance deficit can be attributed to the circuit rather than to motor or sensory side effects. Even a clean replication would support necessity under the tested conditions, not sufficiency, and not the claim that the projection stores a memory. The notice has a narrower procedural implication: the acquisition records for this study cannot currently establish that the compared groups were independent, so the result is unreliable as evidence until independent records or a new study resolve the question. All human review of this draft remains pending, and no live external verification of the archive was performed.

inf-k01.reference_answer: The item reports a well-controlled genome-wide association result: a lead noncoding SNP near gene G is associated with the trait, and several variants in linkage disequilibrium span both G and H. No functional or colocalization data are supplied. The justified conclusion is the locus is associated, and identifying the causal variant and the effector gene requires further evidence. The claim that G is necessarily causal because it is closest, confuses physical proximity with mechanism. Noncoding variants can act on distant genes through chromatin contacts, enhancers and promoters, and the nearest transcript need not be the target. The claim that the lead SNP must be the only causal variant, ignores linkage disequilibrium. The lead SNP is the most strongly associated marker in the sample, but it is a statistical marker for a haplotype; several correlated variants can carry the same association signal, and any of them, or a combination, could be causal. The claim that whole-genome sequencing alone proves the mechanism, confuses variant discovery with functional evidence. Sequencing can find and genotype variants; it cannot show which one changes a regulatory element or which gene is affected. The key principle is that genetic association through linkage disequilibrium is not causality. Three claims should be kept distinct: the locus is associated; a specific causal variant exists and can be nominated; and a specific effector gene and mechanism explain the association. The supplied evidence supports only the first. Uncertainty is substantial. The lead SNP may be a proxy whose true causal variant is badly genotyped or imputed. Fine-mapping depends on the reference panel matching the study population, and mismatch can misplace credible sets. Multiple independent signals may exist at the locus, and conditional analysis is needed to separate them. Ancestry-specific linkage disequilibrium means a signal that maps one way in one population may map differently in another, and winner's curse can inflate the lead effect. Useful discriminating analyses, proposed rather than performed, include conditional association analysis to test for independent signals; statistical fine-mapping with a matched reference panel to produce credible sets; colocalization between the trait association and expression or protein quantitative trait loci in relevant tissues; functional annotation of credible variants, including chromatin state, transcription-factor motifs and allele-specific reporter assays; chromatin conformation data to link candidate elements to promoters; and, most directly, perturbation of the candidate variant in an isogenic system using base editing or CRISPR with appropriate controls. Replication in an independent, ancestry-appropriate cohort strengthens any nominated variant. Each test has a distinct prediction. If a single variant drives the signal, conditioning on the correctly measured causal variant should remove that signal under a correctly specified model; strong linkage can still leave a broad credible set. If the effector is G, colocalization and perturbation of a G-linked regulatory element should track the association. If the effector is H or another distal gene, those same tests should point elsewhere. the supplied evidence establishes a locus association, the linked variants prevent assigning causality to the lead SNP, and G cannot be declared the causal gene from distance or from sequencing alone.

inf-d01.reference_answer: Proposed design. All analysis steps below are proposed; none has been executed. The goal is to identify a reproducible treatment-associated multi-omic program from paired tumor RNA, protein and metabolite measurements, and to explain the distinct roles of integration, enrichment and external validation. M1 states that thirty patients have pretreatment and post-treatment samples. M2 states that RNA and protein were run in different batches and that most post-treatment metabolomics samples share a batch. M3 states that some assays are missing. M4 states that a second small cohort exists and must remain untouched during development. The estimand should be defined at the patient level: the within-patient change from pretreatment to post-treatment, per assay, and the cross-assay program that summarizes those changes. Two goals must be separated: exploratory discovery of shared factors, and predictive or confirmatory validation in independent data. M2 contains the central design threat. If most post-treatment metabolomics samples come from one batch, treatment time point and metabolomics batch are largely or completely confounded. When confounding is complete, no amount of regression adjustment, batch correction, harmonization or multi-omic integration can recover the missing counterfactual, because there are no post-treatment samples measured in the other batch to separate the two effects. The honest options are to restrict metabolomics claims, to treat metabolomics as exploratory, to run a targeted balancing experiment in which paired pre- and post-treatment aliquots are re-measured across balanced batches with shared bridge samples, or to collect a new balanced set. Integration cannot fix a design problem. Observed evidence versus assumptions: the batch structure and missingness are reported facts; the assumption that a shared factor represents treatment biology rather than batch, donor or time is exactly what the analysis must test. Preparation, identity and quality control. Proposed steps: harmonize sample identifiers across all assays so that patient and time point are unambiguous; lock a sample key before analysis; record and verify batch identifiers for every assay; run assay-specific quality control, including RNA integrity, library metrics, protein yield and digest efficiency, chromatographic quality, internal standards and missingness patterns; prespecify quality-control thresholds and exclusion rules; and document clinical covariates such as treatment type, timing, tumor purity and response. Experimental unit, allocation and blinding. The independent unit is the patient, and each patient contributes a paired pre-post observation per assay. Splitting aliquots or samples from the same patient across development and validation partitions is prohibited, because it leaks patient-level information. Proposed allocation: cluster the split by patient, keep the external cohort locked until features and model choices are frozen, and blind the analyst to treatment labels during unsupervised factor discovery where feasible. Sample size should be calibrated: with thirty patients, estimate variance components for patient, batch and residual from a pilot or from technical replicates, then compute the detectable effect size for the prespecified factor-level contrast rather than assuming a power value. If the detectable effect is larger than the biologically plausible effect, the study is underpowered for that contrast, and this must be reported. Intervention and schedule. Sample collection times relative to treatment cycles must be specified by the author and kept consistent; any difference in the pre-post interval across patients is a covariate. Proposed analysis schedule: assay-specific normalization and quality control first; then missing-data handling; then integration; then enrichment; then locked external validation. Integration. Proposed approaches: a multi-view factor model or an explicitly justified late-integration strategy, with the patient-paired contrast as input and assay-specific preprocessing, rather than naive concatenation of all features. Report factor loadings per assay and quantify the association of each learned factor with batch, donor, treatment and clinical covariates. A factor whose variance is dominated by batch or donor structure should not be called a treatment program. Missing assays require an explicit missingness model; complete-case, available-case and imputation analyses should be compared as sensitivity analyses, with the assumption about missingness stated. Enrichment. Proposed approach: use the tested feature universe, meaning the genes, proteins and metabolites that were actually measured and passed quality control, with a dated gene-set or pathway release, and report effect direction and multiplicity. Enrichment against an inappropriate all-gene background can miscalibrate significance in either direction, and a small enrichment p-value does not establish causal direction or mechanism. External validation. Proposed approach: freeze preprocessing, feature selection, factor number and model form before touching the second cohort; then apply the locked pipeline to that cohort and evaluate whether the program reproduces in the same direction with a compatible effect size. Use patient-grouped resampling and nested selection rather than reusing validation data to tune the model. Decision rules: if a factor loses its association when batch-balanced subsets are analyzed, or tracks batch rather than time point, it is not established as a treatment program. If it reproduces in the locked cohort in the same direction, it becomes a candidate reproducible program subject to functional follow-up. If the metabolomics contrast is unidentifiable, report it as such rather than presenting a corrected estimate as though the design supported it. Troubleshooting. Proposed checks: if a factor is batch-dominated, restrict to balanced subsets, add a targeted balancing run, or drop the affected assay from confirmatory claims; if missingness is extensive and non-random, report bounds rather than a point estimate; if factors are unstable across resampling, reduce dimensionality and report stability metrics; if the external cohort is too small to test the full model, prespecify a single primary program-level test instead of many features. Limitations. The design is observational and pre-post, so it cannot separate treatment from time, disease progression or concurrent care; the sample size is small relative to feature count; metabolomics batch confounding may be complete and therefore unfixable computationally; the external cohort is small; and all parameter choices, timelines and effect sizes require author input. Human review remains pending.

required_concepts.criterion: Defines the estimand as a within-patient pre-post treatment contrast per assay and distinguishes exploratory shared factors from confirmatory validation.

Explains that when post-treatment metabolomics samples are mostly one batch, time point and batch are confounded, and that regression or integration cannot recover the missing comparison, so claims must be limited or new balanced data collected.
Requires quantifying each learned factor's association with batch, donor and covariates, and refuses to call a batch- or donor-dominated factor a treatment program.
Keeps every sample from one patient in a single partition, locks the external cohort until preprocessing and feature choices are frozen, and avoids tuning on validation data.
Uses the measured and quality-controlled feature universe with a dated gene-set release for enrichment, reports direction and multiplicity, and denies that enrichment establishes causation.
Addresses missing assays with an explicit missingness model and sensitivity analyses, and prevents imputation or feature-selection leakage from held-out patients.
Treats patients as independent units, preserves pre-post pairing and controls multiple testing, rather than treating features or genes as replicates.
Derives detectable effect sizes from pilot or technical variance instead of inventing a power value, and states decision rules for batch-dominated, non-reproducing and unidentifiable results.

protocol_steps.acceptance_or_stop_rule: If missingness is extensive and non-random, report bounds rather than a single point estimate.

protocol_steps.action: Fit the integration model on patient-paired contrasts.
protocol_steps.variables_and_units: Number of factors; variance explained per assay (percent); loadings per feature.
protocol_steps.control: Permuted or negative-control data; alternative factor numbers.
protocol_steps.acceptance_or_stop_rule: Prespecify the factor number rule and report stability across resampling.

protocol_steps.action: Quantify factor association with batch, donor and clinical covariates.
protocol_steps.variables_and_units: Proportion of factor variance explained by batch, donor, treatment and covariates (percent); confidence intervals.
protocol_steps.acceptance_or_stop_rule: Do not label a factor treatment-associated if batch or donor dominates its variance.

protocol_steps.action: Calibrate detectable effect size from variance components.
protocol_steps.variables_and_units: Variance components for patient, batch and residual; detectable effect size (standardized units); thirty patients (fixed).
protocol_steps.acceptance_or_stop_rule: If the detectable effect exceeds the plausible biological effect, report the study as underpowered for that contrast.
protocol_steps.provenance: proposed; no numeric power or effect size is asserted here

protocol_steps.action: Run enrichment on the tested feature universe.
protocol_steps.variables_and_units: Feature universe (count); gene-set release date; enrichment statistic; effect direction; adjusted p-value or false discovery rate.
protocol_steps.acceptance_or_stop_rule: Reject enrichment computed against all annotated genes rather than the measured universe.

protocol_steps.action: Freeze the pipeline and lock the external cohort.
protocol_steps.variables_and_units: Frozen preprocessing, factor number, feature list and model specification (versioned).
protocol_steps.control: No access to the external cohort until freezing is documented.
protocol_steps.acceptance_or_stop_rule: Stop and restart the analysis if validation data are used for any tuning decision.

protocol_steps.action: Apply the locked pipeline to the external cohort.
protocol_steps.variables_and_units: Direction of effect per factor; standardized effect size; confidence intervals; cohort size (small).
protocol_steps.control: Same pipeline applied unchanged; prespecified primary test.
protocol_steps.acceptance_or_stop_rule: Treat the program as reproducible only if direction is consistent and the effect size is compatible within uncertainty.

protocol_steps.action: Use patient-grouped resampling with nested feature selection.
protocol_steps.variables_and_units: Resampling folds grouped by patient; selection performed within folds (counts); stability metrics.
protocol_steps.control: Permuted outcomes for a null comparison.
protocol_steps.acceptance_or_stop_rule: Discard any performance estimate produced by splitting samples from the same patient across folds.

protocol_steps.action: Apply decision and troubleshooting rules and report limitations.
protocol_steps.variables_and_units: Batch-dominance metric; reproducibility outcome; identifiability status per assay.
protocol_steps.acceptance_or_stop_rule: Batch-dominated or non-reproducing factors are not treatment programs; unidentifiable contrasts are reported as such; only reproducible factors advance to functional follow-up.

Enrichment describes sets of measured features and cannot establish causal direction or mechanism.
All batch layouts, collection timelines and plausible effect sizes require author input; no numeric power, dose or effect value is asserted here.

inf-r01.reference_answer:
The biological question is which genes undergo substantial expression changes between defined biological conditions, especially when only a few independent specimens are available. The methodological question is whether information sharing can reduce unstable estimates without erasing real large effects. These questions are connected but not identical: a numerically stable estimate is useful only if it supports a more reliable biological comparison. The proposal should therefore evaluate effect accuracy, uncertainty, and interpretation rather than declaring success because a plot looks smoother or contains more significant genes.

The hypothesis is that a shrinkage model with suitably adaptive tail behavior can accommodate both many modest effects and a small set of genuine large changes. A competing explanation is that apparent large changes mostly reflect low counts, uncontrolled batches, sample swaps, or a poorly fitted likelihood. Another is that changing the prior simply preserves more noisy extremes. The proposed method must retain strong effects when supported by information while still moderating weakly identified effects. Its benefit cannot be judged only on a favorable set of genes selected after inspecting the results.

Stage one defines the biological contrast. Specify the organism, tissue or cell population, conditions, independent biological unit, and intended effect scale. Record whether the contrast concerns treatment, genotype, time, or an observational association. Define covariates and interactions that are justified by the experimental design. If condition and batch are perfectly confounded, no shrinkage method can identify their separate effects. Such a dataset should fail eligibility for a causal contrast rather than be rescued by an attractive statistical procedure. State that observational expression differences do not automatically identify causal gene functions.

Stage two screens candidate datasets before analysis. Require accessible raw data, a complete sample map, adequate biological replication, interpretable experimental design, and evidence that the selected figure or conclusion is actually supported by the available measurements. Inspect correction or retraction status and unresolved data-quality concerns without equating criticism with fabrication. A highly cited methods article is not sufficient assurance. For a historical forecasting task, only data and methods available at the cutoff may enter the candidate packet. Later datasets may be used privately for validation, with that temporal distinction explicitly labeled.

Stage three freezes a raw-input manifest. Record accession identifiers, filenames, sizes, checksums, sample identities, library type, strandedness, read pairing, and reference versions. Document acquisition failures and mismatches. Confirm that technical sequencing runs from one specimen are not mistaken for independent biological replicates. Preserve an immutable sample sheet and store a separate analysis design table. Every count column must map unambiguously back to its originating raw files. This bookkeeping is scientifically important because a sample swap or duplicated run can create persuasive but incorrect biological differences.

Stage four implements preprocessing in an isolated, versioned environment. Record each tool version, reference genome and annotation checksum, command arguments, random seeds where relevant, and resource limits. Evaluate read quality, contamination indicators, mapping behavior, library composition, and sample-level anomalies using prespecified criteria. If trimming, alignment, quantification, or filtering is changed after examining the primary result, record the change and label the resulting analysis exploratory. Preserve intermediate quality reports and the final count matrix. Failure to complete preprocessing is an execution result, not an invitation to substitute an unrelated processed matrix silently.

Stage five constructs a matched baseline analysis. Use one sample set, one design matrix, one gene annotation, and one defensible count likelihood across estimator comparisons unless a deliberate difference is part of the hypothesis. Confirm the contrast direction and units of effect estimates. Check design-matrix rank and dispersion behavior. Document how size factors or other offsets are estimated and which assumptions they impose about composition. Genes with inadequate information should have their uncertainty represented honestly. Removing them from one method only would bias the comparison.

Stage six defines the proposed estimator independently of the target answer. A plausible route is to replace a thin-tailed effect prior with a heavy-tailed form whose scale adapts to the observed information across genes. Specify which coefficients are regularized and which, such as intercepts, require separate treatment. Describe the likelihood, prior, optimization or approximation procedure, convergence checks, and returned uncertainty summaries. Set parameters using a training or development procedure that cannot inspect the confirmatory test labels. Merely naming a software package is not a method proposal.

Stage seven uses simulations with known effects to make the tradeoff measurable. Vary count abundance, dispersion, sample number, library composition, proportion of changed genes, effect-size distribution, and covariate imbalance over a prespecified grid. Include scenarios that violate the proposed prior's assumptions as well as scenarios favorable to it. Generate independent simulation replicates and retain the seeds. Evaluate absolute error, signed bias, rank recovery, sign errors, and uncertainty calibration across both information and true-effect strata. A single aggregate error can conceal severe failure on rare but biologically important changes.

Stage eight obtains an independent reference for real-data evaluation. A large-replicate experiment can provide a more precise comparison than a small subset, but it is not literal ground truth. Separate the samples used for the small-sample estimate from those supporting the reference whenever possible. If the same observations contribute to both, quantify and disclose the dependence rather than interpreting agreement as independent validation. An orthogonal expression assay or independently collected cohort can strengthen the biological check, with its own measurement limitations and gene-selection rules stated in advance.

Stage nine compares methods under equal conditions. Freeze the gene universe, treatment of zero counts, covariates, scaling convention, and target effect definition. Report performance for all eligible genes and prespecified subsets rather than only the strongest favorable examples. Separate estimation of effect size from hypothesis testing, because a well-ranked list does not prove false-discovery control. Likewise, a low estimated false-sign probability is meaningful only if calibrated in the tested regime. Include runtime, convergence failures, and numerical exceptions instead of dropping difficult cases from the reported denominator.

Stage ten designs figures to test claims rather than imitate appearances. Produce matched estimated-versus-reference effect plots, error-versus-information plots, rank-recovery curves, uncertainty-calibration displays, and sample-quality summaries from stored numerical tables. Fix axis definitions, transformations, limits, and aggregation rules. Retain both the plotted table and the rendering code so that graphical agreement can be traced to underlying values. If reproducing a published figure later, compare numerical quantities and stated conclusions with predefined tolerances; matching colors or panel layout is not evidence of biological reproduction.

Stage eleven examines robustness. Repeat the analysis under justified alternative annotations or preprocessing choices, leaving the primary analysis frozen. Investigate whether a small number of samples, a specific batch, or an extreme count drives the claimed advantage. Use appropriate resampling at the biological-sample level, not independent resampling of correlated technical runs. Assess whether the proposed estimator retains large effects because they are consistently supported across samples or because its prior fails to constrain outliers. Distinguish sensitivity analysis from post hoc tuning to reproduce a preferred result.

The decision rule requires simultaneous improvement in the intended error tradeoff and acceptable uncertainty behavior. Preserving a large estimate is beneficial only when independent information supports its magnitude or direction. A method that improves a few true large effects while greatly increasing false extremes may fail the stated objective. A result confined to simulations generated from its own prior is inadequate evidence of general usefulness. An informative null finding can show that a more flexible prior offers little advantage in a particular information regime; that result still advances the methodological question.

Finally, report a bounded biological interpretation. Improved estimation can help prioritize genes for follow-up, but it does not establish molecular causality, pathway activation from transcript counts alone, or universal superiority across datasets. Distinguish the proposed future research direction from a completed raw-data reproduction: this draft has not downloaded a qualifying dataset, run an end-to-end pipeline, or regenerated an author's figure. Those require an independently audited dataset-and-figure package. For historical matching, the meaningful achievement is the complete argument connecting noisy effects, a justified change in regularization, independent evaluation, and calibrated biological interpretation, not recollection of the later method's name.

inf-p01.reference_answer: Two conclusions must be separated: whether the citation is a real source, and whether the analysis supports a causal pathway. The source question is answered unusually clearly. C2 is a signed provenance record stating that record WG-44 was intentionally invented for a training exercise and was never a journal article. That is affirmative evidence that the citation is fabricated for teaching, not merely unverifiable. It is not an accusation against a real person: the names, journal and identifier belong to the synthetic dossier, and the fabrication is of the record, not a claim about researchers. Because the record was invented, a journal correction or retraction state is not applicable; asking for one would be a category error. The supplied title, with its phrase about proof, should not be allowed to imply that the source carries demonstrative force. The analysis question is separate and fails on its own terms. E1 says cases and controls were sequenced at different centers and have different ancestry distributions. This makes sequencing center, ancestry and case status entangled, and when they are completely confounded no statistical adjustment can restore the missing comparison. Regression, principal components, batch correction and integration can reduce measured imbalance, but they cannot manufacture observations in the missing cells of the design; complete batch confounding is not fixed by regression or integration. E2 compounds the problem: the burden test uses variants passing center-specific filters, and coverage and relatedness are not reported. Center-specific filtering means cases and controls may have been evaluated over different variant sets, so a burden difference can reflect differential callability rather than disease biology. Unreported relatedness threatens the independence assumptions of the test and can inflate significance. E3 adds an enrichment problem: enrichment used all annotated genes rather than genes that could actually pass the study's filters. The background for an enrichment test must be the tested or testable feature universe; using an inappropriate all-gene background can bias significance in either direction and can make an artifactual set look enriched. Given all of this, the dossier does not support a causal pathway claim. Even a robust burden association, properly analyzed, would establish a statistical association that would still need functional and independent evidence before it could be called causal, and burden tests cannot by themselves establish direction or molecular mechanism. Several incorrect alternatives recur. Treating a plausible title as evidence of a real paper is backwards. Treating a smaller burden p-value as evidence that sequencing-center bias is gone confuses statistical significance with design validity. Treating enrichment as establishing causation reverses the inferential order. Inferring deliberate misconduct by a real named researcher from a synthetic record exceeds the evidence and misreads the dossier. Discriminating next steps, proposed rather than performed, are an independent, ancestry-balanced cohort with harmonized joint calling and comparable coverage across groups; relatedness-aware mixed models; restriction of the analysis to matched callable regions with sensitivity analyses; a prespecified enrichment universe with a dated gene-set release and negative-control gene sets; and, only after a robust association is established, targeted functional experiments such as perturbation of candidate genes in relevant models. If the association survives harmonization and balanced sampling, the pathway hypothesis gains support. If it disappears when center, ancestry and callable regions are matched, the original signal was likely structural. the citation is a known synthetic fabrication that should be labelled as such without implicating real people, and independently of that, the analysis cannot support a causal pathway claim.

mol-k02.reference_answer: Observed evidence: the figure presents quantified band intensities from a synthetic knockout validation experiment, not raw blot images. The 50-kDa band falls in the knockout, while the 75-kDa band is unchanged. The 50-kDa band therefore has the stronger genetic specificity support. The alternative claim assigns that support to the 75-kDa band, but a signal that does not change in the supplied validated knockout cannot be said to depend on the target locus; it remains unassigned. The claim that both bands are equally specific, fails for the same reason, because the genotype-specific behavior differs between the two bands. The claim that neither band can ever be assessed by a genetic control, overstates the limitation. Genetic loss is a recognized specificity criterion: if a validated gene disruption removes a band, that band is supported as target-derived in that assay. The support is real but bounded, because knockout validation supports specificity rather than proving it universally, which is why stronger genetic specificity support is preferable wording to proven specific. Several caveats follow from the figure being quantified intensities rather than blots. Saturation, uneven transfer, membrane stripping and antibody concentration cannot be judged from summary bars, so a partial rather than complete reduction of the 50-kDa signal would be hard to distinguish from incomplete knockout or from a mixture of target and cross-reactive signal at the same size. If both bands were quantified on the same membrane and the 75-kDa signal is unchanged, that pattern is consistent with a cross-reacting protein sharing an epitope, a distinct gene product, or a modified species, and this figure does not separate those alternatives. The origin note says the figure is an original synthetic teaching plot generated deterministically, so the values are illustrative rather than a real experiment, and the supplied key is a draft awaiting expert review. Uncertainty therefore includes both biological ambiguity about the 75-kDa species and measurement ambiguity about how the bars were produced. Useful discriminating tests, proposed rather than performed, include an antibody against a different, non-overlapping epitope; immunogen peptide competition; an independent second loss-of-function reagent such as another deletion allele or an inducible degron; epitope-tagged target expression to identify the cognate band; mass spectrometry of the excised 75-kDa band; and target-null cells. The predictions differ: a genuine target species should disappear with independent target-specific perturbations, while a cross-reactive band should persist and should gain no support from those perturbations. the 50-kDa band has the stronger genetic specificity support, the 75-kDa band remains unassigned, and quantified intensities cannot substitute for raw images or orthogonal validation.

bio-k02.reference_answer: The plotted initial-rate curves follow ideal Michaelis-Menten kinetics, and the comparison of inhibitor with vehicle shows the same maximal rate but a rightward shift, so the best description is same Vmax with increased apparent Km. In the simplest scheme this is the signature of substrate-competitive inhibition: the inhibitor raises the substrate concentration required for half-maximal velocity by a factor of one plus inhibitor concentration over Ki, while saturating substrate can outcompete it and restore Vmax. Choice A, lower Vmax with unchanged Km, describes a pattern in which saturation cannot overcome the inhibition, as in noncompetitive or irreversible inhibition, and it does not match shared asymptotes. Choice C, higher Vmax and lower Km, describes activation rather than inhibition. The alternative claim is the important conceptual error: a competitive kinetic pattern does not identify the physical inhibitor binding site. Kinetics reports how rate depends on substrate and inhibitor concentrations under an assumed model; it does not report where a molecule binds. An inhibitor could produce a competitive pattern by binding the catalytic site, but it could also bind an allosteric site that changes substrate affinity, or interfere with a coupled or reporter step in a way that mimics competition. Distinguishing those possibilities requires binding and structural evidence, not another curve shape. The case is synthetic and the supplied key is a draft under expert review, so the plot illustrates ideal behavior. Its assumptions matter: idealized curves exclude substrate inhibition, cooperativity, slow-binding behavior, tight binding when inhibitor and enzyme concentrations are comparable, and assay artifacts such as compound absorbance or quenching. The inhibitor concentration, Ki and experimental fit uncertainty are not supplied. Approximate apparent Km values can nevertheless be read from the plotted curves, as stated below. Uncertainty therefore concerns both model and measurement. Useful discriminating tests, proposed rather than performed, include measuring initial rates across a matrix of substrate and inhibitor concentrations and fitting competitive, noncompetitive, uncompetitive and mixed models globally with confidence intervals; using reciprocal or Eadie-Hofstee displays only as diagnostics, since they distort error structure; checking reversibility by dilution or jump dilution; testing enzyme-concentration dependence to detect aggregation or tight binding, which would require a Morrison-type analysis; and measuring direct binding by isothermal titration calorimetry, surface plasmon resonance or microscale thermophoresis, ideally with a substrate-site mutant to test whether binding and catalysis compete. Competition with a known active-site ligand and structural data would further locate the site. The predictions differ: if inhibition is truly substrate-competitive at the active site, direct binding should be displaced by substrate and a catalytic-site mutation should change inhibitor affinity; if the pattern is allosteric or reporter-based, binding may persist without substrate competition, or the apparent shift may change when the coupled reporter is replaced by a direct product measurement. the plot supports same Vmax with increased apparent Km, which identifies a competitive kinetic pattern under the assumed model, and it does not establish where the inhibitor binds. The plotted axes permit approximate Vmax of 100 nmol/min and apparent Km values near 20 and 60 micromolar to be read from the curves; these are synthetic model values, not estimated parameters with experimental uncertainty. A substrate-site mutation can alter folding or catalysis, so altered affinity needs independent protein-integrity controls.

mol-d02.prompt: Design a proposed experimental protocol to test whether p53 status is necessary under the tested damage conditions and specifically restored by rescue for damage-induced G1 arrest in a same-background isogenic system, while distinguishing true arrest from death or altered composition. Include acute p53 depletion, near-endogenous rescue, matched damage load, live-cell tracking, DNA-content and nucleotide-incorporation measurement, death measurement, caffeine as a separate perturbation, prespecified gating, and a quantitative primary contrast. State all experiments are proposed.
mol-d02.packet: Source summary and curator interpretation (not a quotation): the 1991 record associates p53 elevation with G1 arrest; missing or mutant p53 cells lack the corresponding G1 response; the design compared DNA-damage treatment, p53 status, G1/G2 changes, and caffeine treatment. Its stated limits are that different cell lines and pleiotropic drugs cannot alone prove same-background causation, and that reduced DNA synthesis may reflect death or composition change. Hypothetical constraints for your proposed protocol: one isogenic parental line; acute p53 loss; near-endogenous rescue; a damage agent and caffeine are available but their identities, doses and timings must be calibrated in your protocol; live-cell tracking and fixed DNA-content plus nucleotide-incorporation readouts are available; death must be measured. No historical methods are to be reconstructed.
mol-d02.reference_answer:
All experiments described here are proposed; none is a reconstruction of the 1991 methods. The central design is an isogenic same-background comparison with acute p53 loss, near-endogenous rescue, matched DNA-damage load, live-cell tracking, DNA-content plus nucleotide-incorporation measurement, and death measurement.

Preparation and QC. Establish a parental line carrying a verified wild-type p53 locus and a matched derivative for acute p53 depletion. Because the source does not supply molecular reagents or culture conditions, the protocol must first specify and validate the depletion method and the rescue construct. QC should verify p53 transcript and protein at baseline, after damage, and after rescue by methods orthogonal to the one used for manipulation. Near-endogenous rescue means matching the rescued p53 level to the unperturbed parental range rather than overexpressing; if a quantitative range cannot be obtained from the source, measure it in the parental line and set a predefined acceptable interval. Confirm that the damage agent and caffeine are not toxic in the vehicle arm at the chosen exposure and that the readouts are linear over the relevant range.

Experimental unit, allocation and blinding. The inferential unit is the independently manipulated culture population or independent transduction or knockout event, not an individual cell. Cells within a well are observational units and must be summarized or modelled hierarchically. Randomize wells or culture vessels to damage, caffeine, vehicle, p53-status and rescue conditions with a prespecified allocation table. Blind the person performing imaging and the person scoring cycle and death to condition. If clones are used, do not treat clones as independent p53 replicates unless the p53 manipulation is independently introduced into each background; otherwise clone effects remain confounded.

Handling and analysis sequence. Seed parallel cultures at a density that leaves room for division and tracking. Before treatment, record baseline viability and cycle distribution. Calibrate the damage agent by a dose-time matrix that produces a comparable validated damage signal in p53-competent and p53-depleted cultures; if no independent damage readout is available, this is a required input. Then apply a fixed damage exposure and follow live cells by time-lapse microscopy. In parallel, harvest fixed samples for DNA content and nucleotide incorporation. Measure death in the same wells using an independent viability readout and, where possible, live-cell morphology. The analysis sequence is: first verify allocation and depletion or rescue; second exclude failed manipulations only by prespecified criteria; third quantify live-cell cycle state over time; fourth quantify incorporation in live, death-negative cells; fifth compute G1 occupancy together with entry into S phase and competing death outcomes; sixth compare prespecified contrasts.

Controls. Include vehicle-treated p53-competent and p53-depleted cultures, damage-treated p53-competent and p53-depleted cultures, rescue with and without damage, a non-targeting manipulation control, and caffeine as a separate perturbation arm. Caffeine is pleiotropic, so it cannot be the primary causal evidence; use it to test whether the G1 response is sensitive to a secondary perturbation under matched viability. Include a damage-load control and a death control in every contrast. For incorporation, include a no-incorporation control and a background fluorescence control. For live tracking, include a division-arrested control only if it can be independently validated.

The primary quantitative contrast is the damage-induced change in the fraction of live, death-negative cells in G1, and the reciprocal change in nucleotide incorporation, comparing p53-competent with p53-depleted isogenic cultures; the rescue contrast asks whether near-endogenous p53 restores the parental response. Report effect sizes with uncertainty and the full time course, not only one time point. A secondary contrast is death-adjusted incorporation. Caffeine effects should be reported as a separate interaction, not merged into the p53 necessity claim.

Sample-size and power planning. Use pilot data from the chosen readouts to estimate variance in G1 fraction, incorporation and death. Power should be based on independent culture replicates, not individual cells. If no pilot variance is available, specify a calibration pilot and a required minimum detectable effect; do not invent a number. Because cell-level measurements can be numerous, report both cell-level distributions and culture-level summaries. For live tracking, account for censoring and competing death.

Prespecified exclusions and stopping rules. Flag technical failures of depletion, rescue or baseline viability using rules fixed before treatment. Do not exclude wells merely because post-treatment damage or death differs; report those differences as biological outcomes or unresolved causal mediators. Exclude cells from incorporation analysis if they are death-positive or have ambiguous cycle status; report all exclusions and their counts. Stop or recalibrate if the damage agent produces a different damage load between p53 arms, if death exceeds a prespecified fraction that would make cycle interpretation unreliable, or if the rescue level falls outside the near-endogenous interval. Do not change gates after seeing the primary contrast.

Missing data. Missing wells or lost tracking fields should be handled by a prespecified model that distinguishes missing at random from condition-related loss. If death causes missing cycle data, use a competing-risk or death-adjusted analysis. Do not complete missing values in a way that assumes no death.

Expected results. A positive result would be: damage causes G1 accumulation and reduced incorporation in p53-competent cultures without a matching increase in death; p53 depletion abolishes the G1 response; near-endogenous rescue restores it. A negative result would be no difference in G1 or incorporation after matching damage load and death. An ambiguous result would be a p53-dependent difference accompanied by unequal death, unequal damage load, or a rescue level outside the endogenous range. Caffeine may modify the response but cannot alone prove p53 necessity.

Artifact discrimination. The isogenic design addresses cell-line background confounding. Death-adjusted denominators and live tracking address the possibility that reduced DNA synthesis reflects death or composition change. Damage-load matching addresses unequal injury. Near-endogenous rescue addresses overexpression artifacts. Blinded gating and prespecified analysis address observer bias.

Troubleshooting. If depletion is incomplete, titrate or use an independent depletion strategy and re-verify. If rescue is too high, lower expression until it falls in the parental range. If initial delivered injury differs for a technical reason, recalibrate in a separate pilot; preserve later repair differences as potential biological mediators. If death is high, reduce damage or switch to a live-cell readout that separates death from cycle. If incorporation is low overall, validate the nucleotide pulse and detection system against a positive control.

Conditional conclusion. Only if isogenic acute p53 loss abolishes the damage-induced G1 response and near-endogenous rescue restores it, with matched damage load and without a death or composition confound, should the data support a necessary under the tested damage conditions and specifically restored by rescue role for p53 in this response. Otherwise the result remains an association or is ambiguous. No historical method is reconstructed here.

Curator clarification and operational extension. Loss plus damage-dependent rescue tests necessity and manipulation specificity; it does not establish that p53 alone is sufficient without damage. A separate p53-induction/no-damage factorial arm is needed for sufficiency, with matched expression kinetics and measurement of off-target stress. Choose fixed irradiation or a specified noninfectious genotoxic exposure only after a pilot, and measure initial injury immediately after exposure. Do not match away later differences in repair, which may be caused by p53. Record the original cohort size and longitudinal transitions into S phase, mitosis, quiescence and death; analyzing survivors alone can introduce selection bias. For cytometry, establish compensation and background on independent controls, remove instrument-time anomalies and debris, identify singlets using pulse geometry, and gate DNA content jointly with incorporation using control-derived thresholds fixed before decoding. Confirm S-phase entry with tracked lineages. For a small number of cultures, aggregate or model cells nested within culture and day, avoiding cell-level pseudo-replication. Use a predeclared genotype-by-damage interaction and a separate rescue contrast. Timing must bracket measured damage response and one untreated cell-cycle duration, rather than choosing the most favorable endpoint. A difference in G1 fraction alone does not establish a longer G1 residence time.

bio-d02.prompt: Design a proposed fractionation and reconstitution protocol to test whether a heat-stable separable factor is required for fermentative activity in yeast-juice fractions, while excluding pH, salt, phosphate, dilution and enzyme-damage alternatives. Include defined buffer and ion add-back, protein and volume matching, enzyme-integrity monitoring, independent separation, heat and inactive-analog controls, a quantitative primary contrast, and a conditional conclusion that does not claim chemical structure or NAD identity. State all experiments are proposed.
bio-d02.packet: Source summary and curator interpretation (not a quotation): the 1906 record separates yeast-juice filtrate and retentate, recombines them, and uses boiled extract to compensate; fractions are individually inactive while the combination restores activity, supporting a heat-stable separable factor. The stated limit is that compensation is not chemical structure and does not alone determine NAD identity. Artifacts include pH, inorganic-salt and phosphate changes during separation, and enzyme damage or dilution compensated by nonspecific stabilizers. Hypothetical constraints for your proposed protocol: a yeast-juice-derived fermenting preparation can be fractionated into filtrate and retentate; boiled extract and candidate fractions are available; the active factor is not structurally identified; exact buffer, ion, phosphate, protein, volume and dilution values are unavailable and must be calibrated. All experiments are proposed.
bio-d02.reference_answer:
All experiments below are proposed; none is a reconstruction of the 1906 procedures. The design tests whether a heat-stable separable factor is required for fermentative activity after fractionation, while explicitly excluding pH, salt, phosphate, dilution and enzyme-damage alternatives. It does not claim to identify NAD or any chemical structure.

Preparation and QC. Prepare a single yeast-juice-derived fermenting batch and split it before fractionation so that all arms share the same starting material. Record and calibrate pH, ionic strength, phosphate concentration and protein concentration in the unfractionated control. Because exact values are unavailable, establish working ranges by a preliminary calibration in which the fermentative readout is measured across a matrix of pH and salt or phosphate levels; define a matched window in which the readout is stable. Fractionate by a primary method into filtrate and retentate, and independently by a second method with a different separation principle. QC each fraction for volume, total protein, pH, conductivity or salt proxy, phosphate, and residual unfractionated activity. Monitor enzyme integrity by testing the retained enzyme system with saturating substrate and a validated excess of complementary fraction and by comparing protein patterns or activity before and after mock fractionation; if no independent enzyme-integrity assay is available, specify one as a required input.

Experimental unit, allocation and blinding. The inferential unit is an independent fractionation run from an independent preparation, not an individual assay well. Randomize assay wells to fraction combinations and plate positions with a prespecified allocation table. Blind the person performing the activity assay and the person analysing the curves to fraction identity and to whether a sample is active or control. Use a separately powered confirmation set, with preparation numbers set by a pilot and an explicit precision or power target.

Handling and analysis sequence. Thaw and hold fractions under identical, prespecified conditions. First measure the activity of filtrate alone, retentate alone, and filtrate plus retentate. Then measure boiled extract alone, boiled extract plus filtrate, boiled extract plus retentate, and boiled extract plus filtrate plus retentate. Next run matched add-back controls: a defined buffer at the same pH, the same salt composition and the same phosphate concentration as the missing fraction; a protein-matched but heat-inactivated or inactive fraction; and a volume-matched dilution control. Compare the activity of the recombined fractions with each add-back. Only after the activity is reproducible should a candidate active fraction be purified further and retested in the same reconstitution format. The analysis sequence is: first verify fraction QC; second fit the activity time course; third compute initial rates and endpoints; fourth normalize by total protein and by volume; fifth compare recombination against all matched add-back controls; sixth test the purified candidate against the inactive analog.

Controls. Include unfractionated starting material as a positive control, heat-inactivated fractions, a mock fractionation with no separation, pH-matched buffer, salt-matched buffer, phosphate-matched buffer, protein-matched inactive material, dilution-matched buffer, and a no-add-back baseline. For the boiled extract, include a boiled preparation that has been treated to remove or inactivate the candidate activity if such a preparation can be independently validated; otherwise use heat exposure and mock boiling as separate controls. If an inactive structural analog is available, test it at matched mass and volume; if not, specify the required analog as a calibration input rather than inventing one.

Time and dose calibration. Because no numeric settings are supplied, calibrate the fermentative readout over time to identify the linear initial-rate window. Calibrate the amount of boiled extract and the amount of fraction by a dose series that spans sub-saturating to saturating levels; the primary comparison should use a dose on the linear part of the curve. Calibrate pH, salt and phosphate add-back amounts from the measured composition of the fractions, not from assumed values. If the readout saturates or is unstable, narrow the window before testing the main contrast.

The primary quantitative contrast is the recovery of fermentative activity in the recombined fraction pair compared with the sum of the individually inactive fractions and with matched pH, salt, phosphate, protein and dilution controls. Report absolute product-formation rates at matched original-extract input and final volume, with uncertainty. Protein-normalized rates are secondary because added inactive protein can change the denominator. A secondary contrast is whether the boiled extract effect is heat-stable and separable from the enzyme-containing fraction. A third contrast tests whether a purified candidate reproduces the reconstitution effect while an inactive analog does not.

Sample-size and power planning. Use independent fractionation runs as the unit. Estimate variance from a pilot set of preparations; if no pilot is available, define a calibration pilot and a minimum detectable activity difference. Do not treat replicate assay wells as independent preparations. Power should target the recombination-versus-matched-control contrast, not merely a difference from baseline.

Prespecified exclusions and stopping rules. Exclude preparations with baseline activity outside a prespecified range, with protein loss beyond a predefined fraction, with pH, salt or phosphate outside the calibrated matched window, or with evidence of microbial contamination. Stop or recalibrate if the unfractionated control loses activity, if fractions cannot be matched for pH and salt, or if the readout is not in the linear range. Do not exclude a preparation because it weakens the desired conclusion.

Missing data. If an assay fails, repeat it in the same preparation where possible; if a whole preparation is lost, report it and do not substitute a different preparation without prespecification. Use a model that distinguishes assay failure from true low activity.

Expected results. A positive result would be: filtrate and retentate are individually inactive, recombination restores activity above matched add-back controls, boiled extract supplies heat-stable complementary activity to the enzyme-containing heat-labile fraction, and the effect survives independent fractionation and protein or volume matching. A negative result would be: recombination does not exceed matched controls, or pH, salt or phosphate add-back alone restores activity. An ambiguous result would be partial restoration, activity only in one separation method, or a boiled-extract effect that cannot be separated from protein or dilution effects.

Artifact discrimination. Defined buffer and ion add-back address pH, salt and phosphate changes. Protein and volume matching address dilution and nonspecific stabilization. Enzyme-integrity monitoring addresses operational damage. Independent separation methods address method-specific fractionation artifacts. Heat-inactivated and inactive-analog controls address nonspecific heat-stable material.

Troubleshooting. If recombination fails, check fraction QC and enzyme integrity first. If add-back controls restore activity, the apparent factor is likely a buffer, ion, phosphate or dilution effect. If activity is unstable, narrow the calibrated window and shorten handling time. If the boiled extract is inhibitory, titrate it. If only one separation method shows the effect, treat the result as method-dependent and require independent replication.

Conditional conclusion. If recombination restores activity only when both fractions are present, with matched pH, salt, phosphate, protein and dilution controls, and if the effect is heat-stable and reproducible across independent separation methods, the data support a separable heat-stable factor required for fermentative activity. They do not identify the factor as NAD or establish its chemical structure. If matched add-back controls explain the effect, the conclusion is that the original reconstitution is not sufficient to establish a specific coferment.

Curator clarification and operational extension. Boiling does not replace destroyed enzymes; a heat-stable fraction complements an intact heat-labile enzyme fraction. Test heating the two fractions separately. After cooling, remeasure pH and restore evaporation losses before mixing. Start reactions by adding substrate after equal equilibration; collect blank-corrected carbon-dioxide and ethanol time courses, verifying gas leakage, dissolved-gas equilibration and product standards. Report rate and recovery relative to an equal amount of starting extract at a matched final volume. Monitor the enzyme fraction with excess complementary fraction so a missing cofactor is not misclassified as enzyme denaturation. Treat an inactive structural analog as optional because the factor is not yet chemically identified. Orthogonal chromatography and activity-guided fractionation can test separability before structural identification. A successful reconstitution criterion is an inferential outcome, not a reason to remove negative preparations. Record both failed and successful recoveries. Unexpectedly complete restoration by phosphate or salt is an informative alternative explanation, not an assay failure to be discarded.
