bio-d03.prompt: Design a proposed orthogonal experiment to distinguish catalytic recycling of a citrate-cycle candidate intermediate from pool concentration, respiration alone, or non-cycling activation in a tissue-derived oxidation preparation. Include carbon-isotope pulse tracking, step-specific inhibition followed by validated washout or missing-enzyme restoration, initial pool measurement, no-added-substrate and carbon-balance controls, defined reconstitution, and a quantitative primary contrast. State all experiments are proposed.
bio-d03.packet: Source summary and curator interpretation (not a quotation): the 1937 record combines tissue metabolism, interconversion of candidate intermediates, and small amounts of an intermediate promoting sustained oxidation, leading to a cyclic model. The stated limits are that a small intermediate promoting large oxidation does not uniquely prove a closed cycle, and that the 1937 full text and figures were not read in this evidence package. Artifacts include allosteric activation or bypass stimulation by the catalytic intermediate, and pre-existing tissue substrate pools or enzyme contamination producing apparent catalysis. Hypothetical constraints for your proposed protocol: a tissue-derived oxidation preparation is available; candidate cycle intermediates and a carbon-isotope-labelled substrate can be used; step-specific inhibition followed by validated washout or missing-enzyme restoration are possible; exact intermediate identities, isotope labels, inhibitor names, doses and activities are unavailable and must be specified or calibrated. All experiments are proposed.
bio-d03.reference_answer:
All experiments below are proposed; the 1937 methods and figures are not reconstructed. The goal is to distinguish catalytic recycling of a candidate citrate-cycle intermediate from three alternatives: a pool-concentration effect, stimulation of respiration alone, and a non-cycling activation or bypass. The design uses orthogonal readouts: carbon-isotope tracking, carbon balance, step-specific inhibition followed by validated washout or missing-enzyme restoration, initial pool measurement, and defined reconstitution.

Preparation and QC. Prepare tissue-derived oxidation material from independent biological samples under a single calibrated protocol. Before any intermediate is added, measure the initial endogenous pools of the candidate intermediates and the baseline oxidation rate. If the available preparation contains undefined components, first characterize the baseline carbon balance. QC should verify that the preparation is active, that the substrate is consumed, and that the isotope-labelled substrate is incorporated into the expected products. Because exact intermediates, isotope labels, inhibitors and activities are not supplied, the protocol must specify and validate them before the main experiment. If the candidate intermediate is not chemically pure, purity must be measured and a mock impurity control prepared.

Experimental unit, allocation and blinding. The inferential unit is an independent biological preparation or independent tissue sample, not an individual assay well. Randomize assay wells and positions to conditions with a prespecified allocation table. Blind the person running the assay and the person analysing isotope and carbon-balance data to whether the well received a catalytic amount, a stoichiometric pool amount, vehicle, active inhibitor or inactive inhibitor. Use at least two independent preparations for discovery and a separate set for confirmation.

Handling and analysis sequence. First measure the baseline without added intermediate. Then add the candidate intermediate at a catalytic amount and at one or more stoichiometric pool amounts; the catalytic amount must be calibrated to be small relative to the substrate. In parallel, run a no-added-substrate control, a vehicle control, and a heat-inactivated or otherwise inactive preparation control. Next, pulse the isotope-labelled substrate and follow both the label and total carbon over time. For the cycling claim, track label incorporation into the candidate intermediate and the downstream products, then chase. In a separate arm, apply a stepwise blockade that interrupts the candidate cycle, then restore the blocked reaction and test sustained recovery; downstream metabolite addition is a separate bypass control. Run the same blockade with an inactive analog or without substrate. To separate respiration alone from cycle flux, measure oxygen consumption or an equivalent respiration readout in the same wells, but do not treat it as sufficient evidence of recycling.

The primary quantitative contrast is the oxidation flux and product yield supported by a catalytic amount of intermediate versus the same amount of a non-cycling pool equivalent, after accounting for the initial endogenous pool. The second contrast is label movement from substrate into the candidate intermediate and downstream products in the catalytic arm versus controls. The third is recovery of flux after restoration of the blocked reaction. Carbon balance is a gate: if the measured products and remaining substrate do not account for the added carbon within a prespecified recovery window, no cycle conclusion is made.

Controls. Include no added substrate, vehicle, a stoichiometric pool addition, a heat-inactivated preparation, an inactive structural analog, blockade without intermediate, blockade with intermediate, and a defined reconstituted system containing the key components if available. Measure initial pools in every preparation. Include a respiration-only control in which oxygen consumption is stimulated without label flow through the candidate intermediate. If no defined reconstitution is feasible, state that the design cannot establish closure and treat it as a limitation.

Time and dose calibration. Calibrate the linear window for oxidation and for label incorporation. Calibrate the catalytic dose as the amount that is small relative to substrate and to measured endogenous pools, and the pool dose as the amount that materially changes total pool size. Calibrate the blockade strength so that it inhibits the candidate step without collapsing all oxidation; if the inhibitor is not reversible, use a separate recovery system. If no calibration is possible, specify the required pilot inputs.

Sample-size and power planning. Power independent biological preparations for the catalytic-versus-pool contrast and for the label-flow contrast. Estimate variance from a pilot; if unavailable, prespecify a calibration pilot and a minimum detectable flux or label difference. Do not use assay wells as independent replicates.

Prespecified exclusions and stopping rules. Exclude preparations with poor baseline activity, carbon recovery outside the prespecified window, contamination, or unstable isotope background. Redesign labeling and quantify pool dilution if the endogenous pool obscures the catalytic addition, if the blockade does not inhibit the target step, or if label incorporation is not measurable. Do not exclude a preparation because it lacks the expected effect.

Missing data. Report failed assays and lost preparations. If isotope measurements are missing for a preparation, do not impute a cycle conclusion. Use prespecified handling for samples below detection.

Expected results. A positive cycle-supporting result would show that a catalytic amount of the intermediate increases oxidation and product formation more than a matched non-cycling pool, that isotope label moves through the candidate intermediate into downstream products, that stepwise blockade interrupts this flow, and that restoring the blocked reaction recovers sustained flux within carbon balance. A negative result would show no label flow or no recovery beyond pool effects. An ambiguous result would show increased oxygen consumption without label flow, label flow without catalytic enhancement, or carbon imbalance.

Artifact discrimination. Initial pool measurement addresses pre-existing tissue substrate. Defined reconstitution and enzyme purity checks address contamination. The pool-addition control addresses concentration effects. The respiration control addresses stimulation of respiration alone. The inactive analog addresses nonspecific activation. Stepwise blockade with recovery addresses bypass and allosteric stimulation.

Troubleshooting. If no catalytic effect is seen, verify intermediate purity, dose calibration and baseline pool size. If oxygen consumption rises without label flow, test whether the intermediate is activating respiration or a bypass. If blockade does not recover, verify inhibitor specificity and reversibility. If carbon recovery is poor, improve product separation before interpreting the cycle.

Conditional conclusion. Only if catalytic intermediate addition, isotope flow, step-specific inhibition followed by validated washout or missing-enzyme restoration, and carbon balance all support regeneration of the candidate intermediate should the data support a closed cycle. If the effects are explained by pool size, respiration stimulation, bypass activation or contamination, the result does not establish cycling. The 1937 figures and full text are not available here, so this is a proposed forward design, not a verification of the historical record.

Curator clarification and operational extension. Restoring a blocked cycle requires restoration of the missing reaction. Adding an intermediate downstream of an irreversible block can transiently feed respiration without closing the cycle. Keep this bypass arm separate and test whether activity persists beyond the supplied downstream carbon. Propose a validated isolated-mitochondrial or defined-enzyme preparation, specify a carbon-entry substrate and complementary tracer positions, and inventory oxygen, substrate and cofactor requirements. Use rapid quenching with internal standards, extraction blanks, isotope-purity correction, matrix-matched calibration and recovery controls. Collect densely spaced pilot times, then freeze a sampling schedule spanning initial labeling and several estimated turnovers. Quantify both concentrations and isotopologue distributions of all accessible intermediates, carbon dioxide and major side products. Fit competing cyclic, branched and exchange-only flux models with independently measured uptake/release constraints and identifiability analysis. Label appearing in one intermediate does not prove regeneration; isotope exchange can occur without net flux. Pool dilution is a modeled quantity, not a reason to discard inconvenient tissue preparations. A non-cycling analog cannot be assumed available: use omission and restoration of a defined reaction where chemical analog validation is lacking. Restrict closure claims to the measured reaction system; physiological tissues can run branched or cataplerotic fluxes.

neu-d02.reference_answer:
All experiments below are proposed; the source figure captions are not a protocol and no numeric values are reproduced. The design validates a calcium indicator as an activity readout by pairing it with electrophysiological ground truth and by controlling movement, focus, background and neuropil contamination.

Preparation and QC. Express the indicator in the target cell type and state, and include a structural reference channel in the same preparation. Before recording, verify cell health, baseline fluorescence, expression level and the absence of obvious movement or focus instability. If expression level varies, estimate abundance independently where feasible; calcium-dependent baseline brightness alone is not a pure expression measurement. Because exact indicator identity, expression level, imaging rate and analysis thresholds are unavailable, calibrate the fluorescence-to-spike relationship in the target cell type rather than importing values from another preparation. If a ground-truth electrode cannot be obtained for a particular cell, that cell cannot serve as a calibration unit for spike inference.

Experimental unit, allocation and blinding. The inferential unit for calibration is an independently recorded cell or an independent preparation, depending on the question; cells within one field are not independent replicates for the animal-level claim. Randomize visual-stimulus order and blocks where possible. Blind the analysis of fluorescence to the electrophysiological spike train and blind the spike detection to the fluorescence trace. Keep the allocation of stimulus conditions and analysis gates prespecified.

Handling and analysis sequence. Acquire simultaneous imaging and electrophysiology. Record spontaneous and evoked activity with known or independently detected spike times. Acquire the structural channel throughout. Apply three-dimensional displacement estimation and motion correction before fluorescence extraction. Extract somatic, dendritic and neuropil regions; compute neuropil-subtracted and non-subtracted traces as a sensitivity analysis. Calibrate the indicator with known spike counts across a range of firing rates, then test visual responses. The analysis sequence is: first verify alignment between imaging and electrophysiology; second correct motion; third extract regions and neuropil; fourth estimate spike inference on a training subset; fifth report detection rate, false-positive rate, temporal resolution and amplitude nonlinearity on a held-out subset; sixth compare visual-response detection with and without movement and neuropil controls; seventh test whether expression level changes the calibration.

Controls. Include a structural-reference-only analysis, a neuropil subtraction sensitivity analysis, a movement-corrected versus uncorrected comparison, and a no-stimulus or blank-stimulus control. If an indicator-negative or non-signalling control is available, use it to estimate background and movement artefacts. Use electrical ground truth as the independent benchmark. Include a known spike-count calibration set separate from the test set.

The primary quantitative contrast is the agreement between inferred activity and electrophysiological ground truth across the calibration range, reported as detection and false-positive measures, not merely correlation. The secondary contrast is the visual-response effect size with and without movement correction and neuropil subtraction. A third contrast is whether expression level or indicator kinetics shifts the inferred response at matched spike counts.

Time and dose calibration. Calibrate the imaging rate and analysis window to the indicator kinetics; if the indicator is slow or saturating, report the resulting temporal resolution rather than assuming spike resolution. Calibrate visual stimulus duration and inter-stimulus interval so that responses are separable from movement and from the previous stimulus. Calibrate spike-count ranges in the target cell type. If exact parameters are unavailable, run a pilot calibration and prespecify the accepted range.

Sample-size and power planning. Base power on independent cells or independent preparations for the calibration claim, and on independent animals for any animal-level claim. Estimate variance from a pilot; if unavailable, prespecify a calibration pilot and a minimum detectable change in detection or false-positive rate. Do not inflate n by treating multiple regions from one cell as independent.

Prespecified exclusions and stopping rules. Exclude cells with poor health, unstable baseline, failed motion correction, no ground-truth signal, or expression outside the calibrated range. Stop acquisition for technical timing drift or motion beyond calibrated recovery capacity. Retain saturation and inaccurate spike inference as performance failures, then delimit the validated operating range. Do not exclude cells because their inferred response disagrees with the hypothesis.

Missing data. Report missing electrophysiology, lost frames, or cells without ground truth. Do not impute spike times from fluorescence. For visual-response analyses, prespecify how trials with movement or lost tracking are handled.

Expected results. A positive validation would show that inferred activity tracks ground-truth spikes with acceptable detection and false-positive rates in the target cell type, that visual responses survive movement correction and neuropil subtraction, and that expression level does not dominate the calibration. A negative result would show poor detection, high false positives, or visual effects that disappear after controls. An ambiguous result would show good correlation but poor temporal resolution, or cell-type-specific calibration that does not generalize.

Artifact discrimination. The structural channel and three-dimensional motion estimation address movement and focus drift. Neuropil subtraction sensitivity addresses local contamination. Paired electrophysiology addresses inference error. Expression-level measurement addresses amplitude ambiguity. Stimulus blanks and movement controls address behaviour-related false signals.

Troubleshooting. If motion correction fails, improve the structural channel or stabilise the preparation. If neuropil subtraction removes the signal, quantify the contamination rather than assuming the signal is real. If spike inference is poor, recalibrate in the target cell type or lower the temporal claim. If expression is too high, reduce expression and repeat the calibration.

Conditional conclusion. The data support calcium imaging as an activity readout only within the calibrated cell type, state and expression range, and only for the temporal resolution demonstrated against ground truth. They do not establish that fluorescence equals instantaneous spike output universally. If movement, neuropil or expression confounds remain, the conclusion is limited to a correlative visual response, not a spike-level inference.

Curator clarification and operational extension. The primary calibration is somatic fluorescence against simultaneously recorded somatic spikes. A somatic electrode is not ground truth for local dendritic-spine calcium or synaptic input; a spine-specific claim requires its own validation. Acquire a structural z-stack or volumetric reference before the recording, track reference-plane displacement, and delimit the range over which axial correction is validated. A lone two-dimensional channel cannot reconstruct arbitrary three-dimensional motion. Synchronize acquisition with shared trigger pulses, quantify clock drift, and measure dropped frames. Fix ROI masks and neuropil exclusion rings without consulting test spikes. Fit neuropil coefficients, baseline correction and spike-inference thresholds only on training preparations. Match inferred and electrical events within a preregistered timing tolerance; report precision, recall, false events per recording time, temporal error and confidence intervals clustered by animal. Include silent periods and high-rate trains to assess false positives and saturation. Do not omit saturated or poorly inferred cells simply to improve performance. A calibration that succeeds in held-out trials from the same cell supports a narrower claim than success in held-out animals.

inf-d02.prompt: Design a proposed reproducible bulk RNA-seq differential-expression analysis plan that can be audited without hidden state, including immutable inputs, a sample sheet, reference and annotation versions, count model, contrast and FDR, plot regeneration, and a source-difference audit. The design must keep the experimental unit at the independent treatment allocation level and must not claim execution because no files are supplied. State all analyses are proposed.

The experimental unit depends on independent treatment allocation; donor and well inference are distinct; a single donor cannot identify across-donor heterogeneity merely by adding a donor random effect. The read record is partial, and no actual count matrices, sample sheets or file versions are supplied. Hypothetical constraints for your proposed protocol: a bulk RNA-seq study has treatment and control, possible donors and processing batches, and no files are available at design time. inf-d02.reference_answer:
All analyses below are proposed; no count matrix, sample sheet, reference or result file is available, so no execution is claimed. The plan is a reproducibility and differential-expression design for a bulk RNA-seq study whose inferential unit must be the independent treatment-allocation unit, documenting whether assignment was randomized, not a well or library merely because it has a distinct count profile.

Preparation and immutable inputs. Move all raw sequencing files, sample sheets, reference files, annotation files and code into a read-only project tree before analysis. Record checksums for every file and a manifest that links each checksum to its source and retrieval date. Keep the raw files immutable; all derived files are written to a separate output tree. If files are not supplied, create placeholders that must later be filled with the exact paths, versions and checksums; do not invent them. Preserve the original sample sheet as an immutable object and derive a working sample sheet from it by a scripted transformation.

Sample sheet and experimental-unit QC. The sample sheet must contain, at minimum, a unique sample identifier, raw-file path, condition, independent experimental unit, donor or animal identifier if applicable, processing batch, library batch, sequencing run, and any covariate used in the model. Verify that treatment is assigned at the level of independent allocation. If treatment was assigned to donors but multiple wells or libraries come from each donor, the donor is the treatment unit and wells are subsamples; do not fit a treatment contrast that treats wells as independent treatment replicates. If the design has only one donor, state that across-donor heterogeneity cannot be identified by adding a donor random effect. If the randomization history cannot be recovered, stop the inferential analysis and report the limitation.

Reference and annotation versions. Record the exact genome, transcriptome, annotation and software versions used for alignment and quantification. If the pipeline is alignment-based or alignment-free, record every tool, version, command and parameter. Freeze the reference and annotation before quantification. Run at least one alternative defensible annotation or quantification strategy as a sensitivity analysis, and report whether the primary contrast changes. Do not claim that one strategy is correct by default.

Count model and diagnostics. Fit a count model appropriate to the design, using a negative-binomial generalized linear model with information sharing for dispersion and effect estimation where justified. If the source method is used, record its version and all settings. Check the sample sheet against the count matrix, verify library sizes and count distributions, inspect dispersion estimates, and examine diagnostics for overdispersion, outliers and batch effects. If the design has repeated measures or donors, model the dependence structure at the correct level; standard DESeq2 supports fixed effects, not a generic random-effects formula; a donor random effect does not create donor replication. If the design is simple and independent, do not add unnecessary hierarchy.

The primary contrast is the prespecified treatment effect at the independent experimental-unit level. Define one primary contrast before looking at results. Specify the contrast coefficients, the model formula, the reference level, and the multiple-testing procedure, such as false-discovery-rate control, in the analysis plan. Report effect sizes with uncertainty and the number of independent units. Secondary contrasts are allowed only if prespecified or clearly labelled exploratory.

Plot regeneration and source-difference audit. Every figure and table must be regenerable from immutable inputs by a single documented command. Store the code, session information, package versions and random seeds. Regenerate all plots into a fresh directory and compare checksums or visual summaries with the original. For any difference, audit the source: raw file, sample sheet, annotation, quantification, model formula, contrast, filtering rule, or plotting code. Report the difference and its effect on the primary contrast. Do not overwrite the original outputs.

Controls and calibration. Include positive and negative control samples if the study design provides them; if not, state that they are absent. Calibrate filtering and independent-filtering choices in a prespecified sensitivity analysis, not by optimizing the result. If no pilot dispersion or effect-size estimate is available, specify a calibration pilot and required inputs rather than inventing variance or power numbers.

Sample-size and power planning. Power must be based on independent treatment units. Use a pilot estimate of dispersion and effect size if available; otherwise prespecify a calibration pilot. For donor-based designs, power depends on the number of donors, not the number of cells or libraries. Report the minimum detectable effect under the design and the uncertainty in the variance estimate.

Prespecified exclusions and stopping rules. Exclude samples only by prespecified QC rules, such as failed sequencing, sample-sheet mismatch, or failed library preparation. Do not exclude samples because they change the contrast. Stop the inferential analysis if treatment allocation cannot be verified, if independent replication is absent, if the sample sheet is ambiguous, or if processing is completely confounded with condition and no overlap exists. If batch is partly confounded, report the limitation and do not overstate adjustment.

Missing data. Distinguish missing raw files, missing sample-sheet fields, missing counts and missing covariates. Report each. Do not impute a treatment assignment or a donor identifier. If a covariate is missing for some samples, prespecify a sensitivity analysis rather than silently dropping samples.

Expected results. A reproducible positive result would show the same prespecified contrast and direction across reruns, with a stable FDR-controlled set and sensitivity analyses that do not reverse the conclusion. An inconclusive result may have an interval spanning zero; absence of a biologically meaningful effect requires adequate precision or a prespecified equivalence analysis. An ambiguous result would show a contrast that depends on annotation, quantification or batch handling, or a contrast driven by wells while donor-level replication is absent.

Artifact discrimination. The source-difference audit distinguishes true data differences from code or version differences. The sample-sheet audit distinguishes treatment-unit errors from biological effects. Alternative quantification tests address processing or quantification artefacts. Batch-overlap checks address confounding.

Troubleshooting. If counts do not match the sample sheet, stop and reconcile identifiers. If dispersion estimates are unstable, inspect the design and consider a model appropriate to the unit structure. If batch and condition are confounded, do not claim an adjusted effect. If plots differ, reproduce the difference from raw inputs and document the cause.

Conditional conclusion. Only if the treatment contrast is estimated at the correct independent unit, with immutable inputs, recorded versions, prespecified contrast and FDR, regenerated plots, and a source-difference audit that explains any discrepancies, should the analysis support a reproducible differential-expression conclusion. If independent replication is missing or allocation cannot be recovered, the model output cannot create it.

Curator clarification and operational extension. Before computation, identify the publication, raw-data accession and exact target panels; their absence blocks a claim of paper reproduction. The assessment here is a plan, not a measured pipeline pass. When inputs arrive, verify checksums, read pairing and strandedness; summarize adapter content, quality profiles, alignment/assignment fractions, sample identity, contamination and library complexity. Archive the exact reference release and gene identifier mapping. Feed appropriate raw gene counts to DESeq2, not TPM or already log-normalized expression; for transcript quantification use a documented compatible import that preserves required offsets. Prespecify filtering, size-factor estimation, dispersion fitting, contrast sign, multiple-testing family and FDR threshold. For fully crossed paired samples, a full-rank design such as donor plus condition can account for donor fixed effects. If condition is constant within donor, saturated donor indicators absorb condition; choose an identifiable donor-level design or a suitable hierarchical method instead. Check model rank before fitting. Distinguish inferential tests from effect-size shrinkage and ensure the shrinkage estimator supports the chosen coefficient or contrast. Regenerate PCA from an appropriate transformed matrix, MA and volcano plots from the exact results table, and target gene panels with explicit normalization. Compare numeric data behind plots, not image hashes alone; rendering metadata can change a byte hash while results agree. More reads or wells cannot replace independent biological replication. Ordinary observational designs can still estimate associations when allocation is documented, but randomized causal interpretations require randomization or defensible identification assumptions.

inf-d03.reference_answer:
All experiments and analyses below are proposed; no historical data are reanalysed. The design addresses a study in which treatment is assigned to donors or animals but many cells or fields are measured per donor. The central rule is that the randomized treatment level defines the experimental unit, so cells cannot be treated as independent treatment replicates for a donor-level treatment claim.

Preparation and QC. Before analysis, reconstruct the allocation and splitting history: which donor or animal received which treatment, how many independent donors per arm, how many cells, fields or libraries came from each donor, and whether position or time was aligned with treatment. Build a sample sheet with unique identifiers for donor, cell or field, treatment, batch, position, time and any processing variable. QC should verify that identifiers are unique, that treatment is assigned at the donor level, and that the number of independent units per arm is known. If the allocation history cannot be recovered, the donor-level effect cannot be identified merely by adding a donor random effect to a cell-level model.

Experimental unit, allocation and blinding. The inferential unit for treatment is the donor or animal. Cells, fields and technical measurements are observational units. Randomize treatment at the donor level, using interspersed blocks if spatial or temporal position could matter. If treatment must be applied within a donor, use a within-donor design for a different question and do not describe it as donor-level treatment replication. Blind the person scoring cells or images to treatment and the person analysing the primary contrast to donor identity where possible. Prespecify the allocation table and analysis plan.

Handling and analysis sequence. First summarize each donor, for example as a pseudobulk or donor-level summary, and fit the primary treatment contrast at the donor level. In parallel, fit a hierarchical or mixed model that includes the donor-level treatment effect and a donor-level random effect for repeated cells or fields. For confidence intervals, resample donors rather than cells. For a null distribution, use a null-imposed simulation or exchangeable treatment-label permutation respecting allocation blocks; an ordinary bootstrap is not automatically a null sample. Report both the number of observed cells or fields and the number of randomized units. Then perform held-out validation by splitting donors, not cells, into discovery and validation sets. The analysis sequence is: first verify allocation; second summarize at donor level; third fit donor-level and hierarchical models; fourth run grouped null calibration; fifth report uncertainty at both levels; sixth test position and time confounding; seventh validate on held-out donors.

Controls. Include vehicle or mock treatment, a null calibration in which treatment labels are permuted at the donor level, and a simulation in which the true effect is known. If possible, include a positive-control perturbation at the donor level and a negative-control perturbation. Map position and time for every observational unit. If cells within a donor are split across conditions, include a within-donor control analysis, but label it as within-donor, not donor-level treatment replication.

The primary quantitative contrast is the treatment effect estimated at the donor or animal level, with donors as the independent units. Report the point estimate, interval and the number of independent units. The secondary contrast is the same effect in a hierarchical model; differences may reflect weighting, estimands, link functions or imbalance; investigate them rather than diagnosing dependence from disagreement alone. A third contrast tests whether position or time is confounded with treatment.

Null calibration. Generate a null distribution by permuting treatment at the donor level, or by a parametric simulation that preserves the donor structure and variance components. Use this null to calibrate false-positive rates for the primary contrast. Do not use cell-level permutation, which would assume independence and nullify the correction. If the donor-level null is unstable because there are very few donors, report that the test has low resolution rather than claiming a definitive result.

Held-out validation. Split donors into discovery and validation sets before analysis. Fit the model on discovery donors and evaluate the prespecified contrast on held-out donors. Do not split cells from the same donor across discovery and validation, because that leaks donor-level information. If the number of donors is too small for a split, use prespecified cross-validation at the donor level or state that held-out validation is not feasible.

Sample-size and power planning. Power depends on the number of independent donors or animals, not the number of cells. Estimate variance components from a pilot; if unavailable, specify a calibration pilot and a minimum detectable donor-level effect. Because small independent n affects precision and robustness, report the uncertainty and avoid overinterpreting a significant cell-level test.

Prespecified exclusions and stopping rules. Exclude whole donors only by prespecified health, allocation or QC criteria; exclude cells or fields only by prespecified imaging or measurement quality rules that are applied blinded to treatment. Do not exclude cells because they change the donor-level contrast. Stop or downgrade the claim if treatment is perfectly aligned with position or time, if allocation is unrecoverable, or if the number of independent donors is too small to support the prespecified model.

Missing data. Distinguish missing donors from missing cells within a donor. If a whole donor is missing, do not replace it with cells from another donor. If cells are missing within a donor, prespecify a donor-level summary that is robust to unequal cell numbers, or use a hierarchical model with a missingness assumption. Report all missingness.

Expected results. A robust positive result would show a donor-level treatment effect with a grouped-null-calibrated interval that excludes no effect, with similar direction in held-out donors and no position or time confounding. An unsupported donor-level contrast despite a significant cell-level test may reflect underestimated uncertainty; it does not prove the biological effect is absent. An ambiguous result would show a point estimate similar under cell-level and donor-level models but much wider donor-level uncertainty, or a significant cell-level result that does not survive grouped resampling. Clustering may change uncertainty without changing the point estimate; that is still a valid outcome.

Artifact discrimination. Grouped resampling and hierarchical modelling address dependence. Pseudobulk summaries address cell-level weighting. Position and time mapping addresses spatial or temporal confounding. Interspersed blocked randomization addresses alignment. Donor-level held-out validation addresses overfitting. High intraclass correlation or loss of significance alone does not prove that a biological effect is absent; it changes the unit of inference.

Troubleshooting. If cell-level and donor-level models disagree, report both and do not choose the more significant one. If donor numbers are too small, increase independent donors rather than cells. If position is confounded, use blocked randomization and repeat. If the hierarchical model does not converge, simplify the random-effects structure and report the limitation. If the null calibration is unstable, use simulation with conservative assumptions.

Conditional conclusion. Only if the treatment effect is estimated at the randomized donor or animal level, with grouped null calibration, appropriate hierarchical or pseudobulk comparison, and held-out donor-level validation, should the data support a donor-level treatment conclusion. If the analysis relies on cells as independent treatment replicates, the result is pseudoreplicated for that claim. A non-significant donor-level test with very few donors supports uncertainty, not proof of no effect.

Curator clarification and operational extension. Define the estimand before aggregation: an equally weighted donor-average effect differs from a cell-weighted average when donor cell counts vary. Specify the outcome family and link function. A donor-summary regression on treatment is identifiable with independent donors; a cell-level model containing a separate fixed indicator for every donor cannot estimate a donor-constant treatment term. Use an appropriate random-intercept model only with justified distributional assumptions and enough independent clusters, and inspect convergence and boundary variance estimates. Permute treatment only within exchangeable allocation blocks; preserve pairing where relevant. Enumerate possible assignments when there are few donors and report the attainable p-value resolution. Estimate false-positive calibration across many null-generated datasets, rather than interpreting one permuted dataset as a measured false-positive rate. Simulation assumptions and parameter uncertainty must be explicit. Keep preprocessing, feature selection and thresholds inside each training fold. Cross-validation of prediction is distinct from confirmatory treatment-effect testing; lack of an independent holdout need not invalidate a prespecified correctly calibrated inferential analysis, but it limits external validation. Report the original and cluster-aware estimate with uncertainty and explain why a wider interval is not proof that the original biological claim is false.

mol-r02.original_title: The RAD9 gene controls the cell cycle response to DNA damage in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
mol-r02.later_title: Characterization of RAD9 of Saccharomyces cerevisiae and evidence that its function acts posttranslationally in cell cycle arrest after DNA damage
mol-r02.packet: A yeast study finds that DNA damage delays division in wild-type cells but not in rad9 mutants. An externally imposed division delay permits repair in irradiated rad9 cells. This supports a regulated protective delay rather than a purely mechanical inability to divide. The supplied study does not reveal how the checkpoint is switched on or off. No later molecular mechanism or follow-up result is supplied.
mol-r02.target: Ask whether initiation and recovery of the RAD9-dependent checkpoint require newly synthesized protein or regulation of existing proteins. Block translation with verified inhibition and appropriate toxicity/cell-cycle controls; follow damage-induced arrest and release in wild type, rad9 and rescue. Arrest initiation and recovery under translation block support posttranslational control, without identifying the actual modification. The later report also found constitutive RAD9 transcript rather than irradiation induction.
mol-r02.source_read_depth: Primary abstracts, publication metadata and available figure captions; complete methods/supplements not audited. All detailed experiments are curator proposals.
mol-r02.target_status: Privately sealed retrospective historical target; expert confirmation pending.
mol-r02.prompt: Using only the supplied packet, propose the most valuable next biological question. State competing mechanisms and discriminating predictions. Give an especially detailed, ordered and auditable proposed research plan, including prerequisites, calibration, independent units, allocation/blinding where applicable, controls, measurements, analysis, stop rules and troubleshooting. Explain positive, negative and ambiguous outcomes and the strongest justified conclusion. Distinguish proposals from reported results; do not invent missing author methods. This is one independent attempt without feedback.
mol-r02.reference_answer:
The useful next question is whether the checkpoint can be initiated and released using existing cellular proteins, or whether new protein synthesis is required. The original observations establish a RAD9-dependent protective delay, not the biochemical switching mechanism. The competing models predict different responses to an independently verified translation block. This proposed experiment should measure checkpoint initiation and recovery separately; failure to divide during drug exposure alone is not evidence of checkpoint function because translation inhibition can arrest growth for unrelated reasons.

First assemble matched wild-type, rad9 loss-of-function and near-endogenous complementation strains. Confirm strain identity, genotype, basal growth, DNA content and viability. Use independent cultures initiated separately, with culture/day as the replication level and cells as nested observations. Include an independent genetic perturbation or allele when feasible. Document the exact strain background and complementation expression before choosing exposure conditions. Confirm that fluorescent tags or reporters do not change the baseline damage response. No historical dose, strain sequence or timing is available in the packet; those are prerequisites to record, not numbers to invent.

Calibrate a noninfectious DNA-damage exposure in a separate pilot to produce a detectable, reversible checkpoint response in wild type. Measure initial injury and viability before substantial genotype-dependent repair occurs. Independently titrate a translation inhibitor, such as cycloheximide, to suppress labeled-amino-acid incorporation over the intended observation window while preserving recoverable viability. Measure residual translation quantitatively and report the assay detection limit. Confirm that the inhibitor does not interfere with the damage assay or fluorescent reporters. Maintain a vehicle/no-damage control for every genotype and inhibitor condition.

Randomize cultures within day to a genotype-by-damage-by-translation-block factorial design. For initiation, establish translation inhibition before the damage challenge and verify it throughout the window. For maintenance and recovery, first allow checkpoint arrest to develop, then apply translation inhibition in a separate arm. Follow matched undamaged cultures under the same drug schedule. A third schedule removes the inhibitor after the observation period to establish recoverability. If a physical cell-cycle synchronization procedure is used, validate its own stress response and include asynchronously growing cultures as an orthogonal check.

Acquire time-lapse records with a validated cell-cycle readout and parallel DNA-content and budding/morphology measurements. Score first division, nuclear segregation, arrest duration and death for the original cohort, not only surviving cells. Collect damage-repair measurements at prespecified times alongside translation assays. Set sampling intervals from the pilot so several measurements span the shortest relevant transition. Blind tracking and morphology scoring to genotype and treatment; retain raw movies, field-selection rules and failed tracks. Resolve ambiguous events with a second blinded scorer rather than choosing favorable cells.

The initiation contrast is the damage-specific additional delay in translation-blocked wild type relative to its undamaged drug control, compared with the corresponding rad9 contrast. The recovery contrast asks whether cells exit the checkpoint as damage resolves despite persistent verified translation suppression. Because the drug can suppress general cell-cycle progression, an interpretable checkpoint-specific marker or an orthogonal reversible perturbation may be necessary; merely seeing no division under drug cannot identify checkpoint maintenance. Quantify recovery after drug removal separately from recovery during the block.

Use survival or multistate analysis with death as a competing event and clustering by independent culture. Prespecify the primary interaction, a biologically meaningful delay and a precision or power target from pilot variance. Do not count hundreds of cells as hundreds of independent cultures. Report every treatment trajectory and uncertainty. Technical exclusions include failed strain identity, failed exposure or unusable imaging under rules fixed before unblinding. Incomplete translation suppression and excessive nonspecific toxicity make the mechanistic test inconclusive; they are not grounds to replace inconvenient outcomes with favorable repeats.

Checkpoint initiation and damage-associated recovery during a sufficiently sensitive translation block, with RAD9 dependence and appropriate drug controls, support regulation of pre-existing proteins. They do not identify phosphorylation or prove that absolutely no new protein is needed below the assay detection limit. Failure under the inhibitor could instead reflect toxicity, loss of energy or depletion of a short-lived permissive factor. Use an orthogonal acute translation perturbation and measure metabolic competence before attributing necessity to new synthesis. Constitutive RAD9 transcript would complement this argument but would not by itself establish posttranslational control.

The sealed later study by Weinert and Hartwell reports arrest induction and recovery in the presence of cycloheximide and interprets this as posttranslational regulation. A qualified historical-direction hit requires the biological switching question, a verified synthesis perturbation, separate initiation/recovery readouts and the appropriate conditional prediction. Naming RAD9 or the later article without this experiment is not a hit. A different well-identified mechanistic proposal can earn scientific-quality credit even if it does not match this historical direction. Full original methods remain unaudited, so the operational plan above is explicitly a proposed design.

mol-r03.original_title: Cleavage of GSDMD by inflammatory caspases determines pyroptotic cell death
mol-r03.later_title: Pore-forming activity and structural autoinhibition of the gasdermin family
mol-r03.packet: Inflammatory caspases cleave gasdermin D. Genetic loss and fragment-expression experiments link this processing to pyroptotic cell death, with the amino-terminal portion carrying cytotoxic activity. These observations do not, on their own, reveal what physical action the fragment performs or whether another cellular component executes membrane injury. No subsequent purified-protein membrane experiments are supplied.
mol-r03.target: Determine whether released gasdermin-N directly binds lipids and forms membrane pores, and whether the C-terminal domain restrains this activity. Purify validated full-length/N/C and cleavage-resistant proteins, compare liposome leakage across controlled lipid compositions, image pores and test structure/function mutants in cells. Direct reconstitution plus orthogonal pore evidence and selective loss-of-function separates intrinsic pore formation from indirect cellular death. Distinguish early permeabilization from terminal rupture. The 2016 erratum only corrects the manuscript received date: https://www.nature.com/articles/nature20106.

Give an especially detailed, ordered and auditable proposed research plan, including prerequisites, calibration, independent units, allocation/blinding where applicable, controls, measurements, analysis, stop rules and troubleshooting. mol-r03.reference_answer:
The unresolved question is what physical activity the released gasdermin amino-terminal fragment performs: does it directly permeabilize a lipid membrane, or activate another cellular executor? A related mechanistic question is whether the carboxy-terminal region inhibits that intrinsic activity. Cell death after fragment expression cannot distinguish these models. The highest-information next stage is a minimal reconstitution with orthogonal evidence of membrane pores, followed by controlled structure-function tests in cells. All procedures below are proposed; no unreported result or exact author setting is asserted.

Define the species, sequence, cleavage boundary and validated protein constructs before production. Prepare full-length protein, amino-terminal fragment, carboxy-terminal fragment, cleavage-resistant full-length protein and a deliberately inactive control whose folding can be checked. Record tags and purification history. Verify identity, purity, concentration, aggregation state and integrity with independent measurements. Compare tag-free or alternative-tag preparations when the tag could obstruct membrane binding. Use at least two independent protein preparations and several independent liposome preparations; technical wells do not substitute for these units.

Construct a prespecified lipid-composition panel that includes a baseline membrane and membranes differing in candidate charged lipids while controlling total lipid concentration and vesicle size. Validate vesicle size/dispersity and encapsulation of a soluble reporter. Remove unencapsulated reporter before measurements. Include no-protein, buffer-only, inactive-protein and complete-disruption controls to define zero and maximal release. Test protein preparations directly against free reporter to detect fluorescence quenching or enhancement. Any protease used for cleavage requires protease-only and matched carryover controls.

In a pilot, vary protein-to-lipid ratio and observation duration to identify a range where kinetics can be resolved before the reporter saturates. Freeze these settings before the confirmatory comparison. Randomize plate positions and blind the preparation codes. Compare full length, cleaved full length, amino-terminal fragment, carboxy-terminal fragment and cleavage-resistant protein under identical conditions. Follow leakage continuously, subtract matched blanks and normalize against the detergent-defined dynamic range. Record spontaneous leakage and discard only technical liposome failures according to prespecified criteria, not a lack of the desired protein effect.

Leakage is not sufficient evidence of a discrete pore: nonspecific detergent-like disruption or aggregates may also release dye. Add an orthogonal structural readout, such as validated membrane imaging, and a size-selective permeability assay using independently calibrated reporters. Measure membrane association with an assay that separates free aggregates from membrane-bound material and include liposome-free controls. Analyze pore or lesion counts without selecting only illustrative fields. If reliable structural resolution is unavailable, report direct permeabilization and leave pore architecture unresolved.

Test candidate membrane-binding or oligomerization substitutions guided by justified structural information. Confirm equal protein integrity and folding before comparing functional loss; a misfolded mutant cannot identify a specific interface. Assess concentration-dependent inhibition by the carboxy-terminal region and compare with matched unrelated protein. An isolated-domain interaction or artificial in-trans inhibition is not automatically equivalent to native intramolecular autoinhibition. Combining cleavage dependence, full-length inactivity, fragment activity and structurally interpretable mutations gives a stronger argument than any one result.

In a complementary noninfectious cellular model, use matched loss-of-function and rescue backgrounds with expression near the validated endogenous range. Verify localization and cleavage independently. Measure small-solute permeability, morphology, viability and release of a larger cytosolic marker over time. Separate early permeability from terminal rupture; a pore-forming fragment need not execute every subsequent lytic event. Include expression-only, inactive-mutant and instrument-background controls. Rescue differences must be interpreted alongside protein abundance and general cell health, not simply the nominal construct identity.

Prespecify the primary fragment-versus-full-length leakage contrast and the mutant-versus-intact contrast, with preparation-level uncertainty and multiplicity control for the lipid panel. Base sample size on pilot preparation variability and a meaningful permeability difference. Retain negative preparations and confidence intervals. If all samples leak, revisit vesicle stability; if only aggregated protein leaks, improve purification and reassess; if mutants lose folding, redesign the comparison. If cell effects persist but reconstitution fails despite validated positive controls, a missing cofactor or indirect mechanism remains plausible.

The strongest supportive outcome is lipid-dependent permeabilization by purified amino-terminal protein, independently observed membrane pores, and matched structure-function effects in cells. bio-r02.original_title: Direct observation of the rotation of F1-ATPase
bio-r02.later_title: F1-ATPase is a highly efficient molecular motor that rotates with discrete 120 degree steps
bio-r02.packet: A fluorescent filament attached to the central subunit of immobilized F1-ATPase rotates in the presence of ATP. This demonstrates rotary motion in the isolated enzyme. The supplied observation does not resolve elementary mechanical events, their relation to nucleotide turnover, or how the marker load changes observed motion. No later stepping or energetic measurements are provided.
bio-r02.target: Ask how ATP chemistry couples to discrete angular motion. Resolve angular trajectories over ATP concentration and probe load, calibrate temporal/angular response, quantify steps and dwell distributions and estimate drag/work with uncertainty. A resolved approximately 120-degree stepping pattern and ATP-dependent waits support sequential catalytic coupling; work per step near one ATP hydrolysis free energy requires an explicit biochemical free-energy estimate and load calibration, not assertion from rotation alone.
bio-r02.source_read_depth: Primary abstracts, publication metadata and available figure captions; complete methods/supplements not audited. All detailed experiments are curator proposals.
bio-r02.target_status: Privately sealed retrospective historical target; expert confirmation pending.
bio-r02.prompt: Using only the supplied packet, propose the most valuable next biological question. State competing mechanisms and discriminating predictions. Give an especially detailed, ordered and auditable proposed research plan, including prerequisites, calibration, independent units, allocation/blinding where applicable, controls, measurements, analysis, stop rules and troubleshooting. Explain positive, negative and ambiguous outcomes and the strongest justified conclusion. Distinguish proposals from reported results; do not invent missing author methods. This is one independent attempt without feedback.
bio-r02.reference_answer:
The next question is how ATP turnover couples to elementary rotation: is motion made of reproducible angular steps separated by chemical waits, and does each mechanical event correspond to a nucleotide-dependent transition? The original rotation movie shows a motor, but cannot resolve this coupling or establish efficiency. Competing explanations include continuous rotation blurred by the reporter, discrete chemical stepping, and apparent pauses caused by surface contacts or probe drag. A proposed single-molecule experiment should manipulate ATP availability and mechanical load independently.

Specify the F1 construct, immobilization geometry and reporter attachment sites, then validate bulk ATPase activity before and after labeling. Confirm that the chosen attachment reports the central rotating subunit rather than nonspecific surface motion. Use independent enzyme and flow-cell preparations. Record the fraction of immobilized molecules that are inactive, irregular or trackable; analyzing only attractive rotating molecules biases the population description. Inactive enzyme, ATP-free buffer and nonspecific attachment controls help establish the motion background.

Calibrate angle estimation using a known geometric or driven-motion reference, camera timing, exposure duration and localization noise. Measure photobleaching, drift and tracking errors under the intended illumination. Verify that frame rate and reporter response can resolve the predicted dwell duration. Pilot ATP concentrations from a regime with long resolvable waits to a faster regime, while holding other buffer components fixed. Record free magnesium and nucleotide composition where relevant; nominal ATP alone may not define substrate availability. Do not claim a particular historical concentration from the supplied packet.

Prepare a reporter-load series with measured geometry. Shorter/lighter probes reduce drag but can reduce angular precision; larger probes improve tracking yet may limit speed or distort steps. Randomize measurement order across ATP and reporter conditions and blind trajectory analysis. Image sufficiently long to observe repeated cycles without selecting duration based on a desired step pattern. Use predefined tracking quality and surface-contact rules. Where possible observe the same molecule across controlled solution changes, while retaining an independent-preparation comparison to detect drift or irreversible loss.

Retain raw image sequences, localization outputs and time stamps. Estimate angles and unwrap rotations using a method tested on synthetic trajectories with known steps and on a continuous-motion null. Fit candidate step-and-dwell models and continuous-motion models without fixing the answer to 120 degrees. Assess missed steps, merged waits and apparent backward motion caused by localization noise. Compare inference across frame rates and independent algorithms. A peak created by a three-state prior is not evidence for three catalytic steps.

Estimate angular increments, dwell-time distributions, rotation speed and backward-event frequency at each ATP concentration and load. Under an ATP-binding-limited model, waits should shorten with increasing ATP over the appropriate range while a characteristic angular increment remains. A load-dependent transit time should be distinguished from a chemistry-dependent waiting time. Fit explicit kinetic alternatives and examine residuals and parameter identifiability. Histograms alone cannot show that every wait corresponds to exactly one ATP molecule; compare the mechanochemical model with independently measured turnover where feasible.

For energetics, calibrate rotational drag or applied torque in the actual geometry, including proximity to the surface and reporter shape. Integrate torque over angular displacement to estimate mechanical work with propagated uncertainty. Estimate ATP-hydrolysis free energy using the actual nucleotide and phosphate activities, temperature and solution conditions, not a universal textbook number. Distinguish work per step, dissipated work, average mechanical power and total chemical consumption. Near equality under one load does not establish perfect efficiency at all loads, nor ATP synthesis during reverse rotation.

Use molecule as a nested unit within enzyme/flow-cell preparation. Prespecify a primary test of ATP-dependent dwell times and a separate test of angular-step consistency across valid loads. Base independent preparation numbers and molecule counts on a precision target with between-preparation variability. Report all exclusion reasons, raw traces and sensitivity to step-detection thresholds. If steps disappear only at low frame rate, improve acquisition rather than concluding continuity. If pauses track reporter size or surface position, investigate mechanical hindrance. If both ATP and load vary together, the experiment cannot separate chemical from mechanical limitations.

A robust outcome would show reproducible discrete increments near one-third of a revolution, ATP-dependent waiting behavior and a quantitatively supported work-to-free-energy comparison. It would support sequential coupling in isolated F1 under the tested conditions. It would not automatically establish behavior of membrane-coupled FoF1 in a cell. The sealed Yasuda and colleagues paper reports approximately 120-degree steps and work near the free energy of one ATP hydrolysis. A historical-direction hit requires resolved stepping, ATP/load discrimination and the corresponding prediction, with credible measurement controls; reciting the angle or article title alone is insufficient.

neu-r02.original_title: Receptive fields, binocular interaction and functional architecture in the cat's visual cortex
neu-r02.later_title: Single-cell responses in striate cortex of kittens deprived of vision in one eye
neu-r02.packet: Recordings in visual cortex reveal organized receptive fields and neurons influenced by the two eyes. Describing this organization does not establish how visual experience contributes to its development. The supplied observations contain no developmental perturbation, recovery experiment, or later deprivation result. Any animal work in a proposed plan must use an approved welfare-reviewed design and an explicit justification for model and intervention.
neu-r02.target: Ask whether early visual experience determines cortical responsiveness to each eye. Compare controlled unilateral visual deprivation with normally reared/sham controls, calibrated stimulation of each eye separately, and blinded cortical single-unit sampling. Test the distribution of ocular dominance across animals, while ruling out persistent optical, retinal and thalamic defects. A shift toward the experienced eye supports experience-dependent cortical organization; it does not alone localize a synapse or establish the entire critical-period curve.

Give an especially detailed, ordered and auditable proposed research plan, including prerequisites, calibration, independent units, allocation/blinding where applicable, controls, measurements, analysis, stop rules and troubleshooting. neu-r02.reference_answer:
The useful biological question is whether early patterned visual experience helps establish the distribution of cortical responsiveness to the two eyes. Adult organization alone cannot distinguish an experience-independent developmental program from experience-dependent modification. A discriminating proposal compares controlled alteration of one eye's visual experience with matched rearing controls and tests each eye independently after optical access is restored. The endpoints are cortical response distributions and competing peripheral explanations, not an assumption that all reduced responses reflect cortical rewiring.

Before work, justify the model and developmental stage using available evidence and obtain an approved welfare-reviewed protocol with veterinary endpoints. Do not reconstruct historical deprivation procedures from an abstract. Specify the approved reversible manipulation, monitoring schedule and stopping criteria from that protocol. Consider whether existing data or a less invasive validated manipulation can answer the question. The packet does not supply animal numbers, exposure duration, anesthesia, recording coordinates or optical parameters; these must be justified and documented before execution.

Allocate independent animals within litter and developmental-stage blocks to altered visual experience, sham handling and normal experience, balancing sex or other justified covariates. Counterbalance which eye is affected. A bilateral-experience-control arm may help separate interocular competition from general visual deprivation, but its interpretation and welfare cost require a specific justification. Animals, not recorded neurons, are independent treatment units. Randomize recording order and maintain blinded group codes for stimulus presentation, unit selection and analysis.

Document baseline ocular health and the effectiveness of the experience manipulation using independent observations. Monitor optical clarity and general development throughout. At the prespecified endpoint, verify that both eyes can transmit the test stimulus comparably; persistent obstruction cannot be called cortical plasticity. Record refraction or alignment where relevant and control illumination, contrast and retinal stimulus position. Use independent retinal or visual-pathway measurements to evaluate peripheral function when the cortical responses differ. A normal-looking eye does not by itself prove normal retinal signaling.

Map receptive fields before presenting a randomized, counterbalanced stimulus set to each eye separately. Match stimulus luminance, contrast, orientation coverage and timing across eyes. Include blank trials, repeated stimuli and eye-isolation controls to prevent unintended stimulation of the other eye. Record neural signals using fixed depth/position sampling rules that do not depend on finding a desired ocular preference. Establish unit isolation, response reliability and baseline stability criteria before decoding treatment labels. Retain neurons without a visually evoked response in a separately reported category rather than silently deleting them.

For each qualified unit, quantify baseline-corrected responses from each eye, orientation tuning and reliability with uncertainty. Define a bounded ocular-dominance index only when its response denominator is sufficiently measurable; weak responses need an explicit category rather than an unstable ratio. Report distributions per animal and the proportions of contralateral, ipsilateral, binocular and unresponsive units. Use a hierarchical model or animal-level distributional contrast, with sampling location as a documented nuisance variable. Do not let animals with many recorded neurons dominate the treatment estimate.

Prespecify a primary shift in the ocular-dominance distribution and a meaningful animal-level effect. Use pilot between-animal variability to plan power or precision. Record litter, developmental stage, recording site and all technical losses. Blinded technical exclusions may address recording instability or failed stimulus isolation; an animal with a weak deprivation effect must remain an outcome. Report deviations from the approved protocol. If peripheral deficits prevent an equivalent retinal stimulus, the localization question is unresolved even when the cortical group contrast is large.

A systematic shift toward the experienced eye, with validated input to both eyes and controlled cortical sampling, supports experience-dependent organization. It does not by itself identify a synaptic site, eliminate thalamic contributions or establish the full developmental sensitive period. To localize further, compare cortical effects with upstream physiological measurements. To test timing or recovery, run separately powered developmental-onset or restoration cohorts; neither can be inferred from one endpoint. A null group contrast may reflect insufficient manipulation or low precision and should be interpreted with manipulation checks and intervals rather than as proof of an innate immutable circuit.

The sealed Wiesel and Hubel follow-up measured cortical responses after monocular visual deprivation. A qualified historical-direction match requires the developmental-experience question, controlled unilateral manipulation, eye-specific cortical recording and the predicted relative ocular-response change with peripheral and sampling controls. Merely proposing more receptive-field recordings or naming a famous critical period does not qualify. Equivalent approved designs can receive quality credit. This is a proposed modern audit of causal logic, not a claim that all historical animal procedures or all supporting methods have been reviewed.

neu-r03.original_title: Dopamine neurons report an error in the temporal prediction of reward during learning
neu-r03.later_title: Discrete coding of reward probability and uncertainty by dopamine neurons
neu-r03.packet: During learning, dopamine-neuron responses to rewards diminish as rewards become predicted. Unexpected timing produces activation, while omission at an expected time produces a depression. These observations connect neural activity with violations of reward prediction. They do not establish whether activity during the waiting period carries additional information about variable outcomes. No later probability-manipulation experiment or result is included.
neu-r03.target: Separate expected reward from outcome uncertainty with cue-conditioned reward probabilities including 0, intermediate probabilities and 1. Analyze phasic cue/outcome responses separately from delay-period firing, tracking movement and licking. The later direction is delay activity greatest near probability one half, separable from phasic prediction signals. Counterbalance cues, test matched expected-value distributions, model learning/history, and avoid claiming causal necessity from recordings.
neu-r03.source_read_depth: Primary abstracts, publication metadata and available figure captions; complete methods/supplements not audited. All detailed experiments are curator proposals.
neu-r03.target_status: Privately sealed retrospective historical target; expert confirmation pending.
neu-r03.prompt: Using only the supplied packet, propose the most valuable next biological question. State competing mechanisms and discriminating predictions. Give an especially detailed, ordered and auditable proposed research plan, including prerequisites, calibration, independent units, allocation/blinding where applicable, controls, measurements, analysis, stop rules and troubleshooting. Explain positive, negative and ambiguous outcomes and the strongest justified conclusion. Distinguish proposals from reported results; do not invent missing author methods. This is one independent attempt without feedback.
neu-r03.reference_answer:
The unresolved question is whether neural activity represents uncertainty about an outcome separately from its expected value and from a brief prediction error. The original packet describes responses around unexpectedly delivered or omitted rewards. A new experiment can vary cue-conditioned reward probability and examine activity during anticipation separately from cue and outcome transients. A useful hypothesis predicts a nonmonotonic uncertainty-related signal, whereas a value signal should track expected reward under matched outcome magnitudes. These are competing interpretations to test, not results already present in the packet.

Specify an approved behavioral preparation, neural recording method and objective criteria for identifying the relevant neuron population. If physiological features are used without definitive molecular identification, preserve that uncertainty in the claim. Establish reward delivery calibration, cue timing, eye or body tracking and synchronized acquisition clocks. Verify delivered reward volume or magnitude on independent test trials. Record behavioral engagement, licking and movement so that motor preparation and arousal can be considered rather than assigned to neural uncertainty by default.

Train distinct counterbalanced cues associated with a probability grid that includes zero, one and intermediate values. Keep the nominal reward magnitude and cue-to-outcome interval fixed for the primary probability series. Randomize trial order within blocks and ensure enough trials to estimate both rewarded and unrewarded outcomes at intermediate probabilities. Verify learning with independent behavioral measures and model trial history. Do not exclude slow-learning subjects after inspecting the neural effect; define training and analysis rules prospectively.

A fixed-magnitude probability series changes expected value and variance together, so it does not by itself isolate uncertainty. Add a prespecified complementary condition set that matches expected value across different reward distributions, with practical probability and magnitude combinations. Avoid relying only on a visually distinctive cue at probability one half. Counterbalance cue identities across subjects, include familiar sensory controls and check salience. Matching expected value may alter magnitude-related sensory or motivational effects, so compare multiple matched pairs and report remaining nonidentifiability.

Record baseline, cue onset, anticipation, expected outcome time and post-outcome activity in every trial. Choose analysis windows from independent pilot data or timing rules, not the largest observed difference. Quantify phasic cue responses, outcome prediction-error responses and sustained or ramping delay activity separately. Keep rewarded and unrewarded intermediate-probability trials in the anticipatory analysis; splitting only on a later outcome can produce selection artifacts. Track movements and licks with the same clock and examine whether neural differences precede or simply follow them.

Fit explicit models containing expected reward, candidate uncertainty measures, recent outcomes, trial number and measured behavior, allowing appropriate subject and neuron dependence. Compare predictive performance on held-out blocks or sessions. Probability one half maximizes Bernoulli outcome variance for fixed magnitude, but several uncertainty constructs can yield related patterns; distinguish a particular model from a general uncertainty label. Correlated regressors can make coefficients unstable even when a model fits well. Report uncertainty, alternative model comparisons and their sensitivity to behavioral covariates.

Prespecify the primary nonmonotonic anticipatory contrast, such as intermediate probability against endpoints, together with monotonic value-related contrasts. Base sample-size planning on independent subjects and sessions with nested neurons, not solely on thousands of trials. Plan exclusions for failed timing, unstable recordings and failed reward delivery before group decoding. Preserve all valid neurons selected by the independent population-identification rule. Missing behavior tracking limits confound adjustment and must be reported rather than imputed from the neural trace.

A strong supportive outcome is delay activity highest around uncertain intermediate outcomes, replicated across cue identities and informative value-matched comparisons, while phasic responses follow prediction-related patterns. This supports separable neural correlates under the tested conditions. It does not establish that the activity causes learning, risk preference or attention. A causal extension would require a temporally restricted perturbation and controls for movement, motivation and sensory processing, with a behavioral prediction specified in advance. If the apparent uncertainty signal disappears with appropriate timing or cue controls, revise the mechanism rather than selecting a favorable recording subset.

The sealed Fiorillo, Tobler and Schultz paper reports a gradual delay-period response covarying with outcome uncertainty and distinguishes it from phasic responses. A qualified hit requires the uncertainty-versus-value question, probability manipulation, temporally separated neural readouts and a prediction distinguishing intermediate probabilities from endpoints. A name, a citation or a generic proposal to study dopamine is insufficient. Scientifically rigorous alternative next questions can receive quality points without a historical hit. The proposed controls exceed the narrow historical summary and are not attributed to unreviewed author methods.

inf-r02.original_title: Simultaneous epitope and transcriptome measurement in single cells
inf-r02.later_title: Integrated analysis of multimodal single-cell data
inf-r02.packet: Oligonucleotide-tagged antibodies allow selected surface-protein measurements and transcript measurements to be linked to the same single cells. The two measurements can provide complementary information and have different noise and detection properties. The supplied result establishes joint measurement, but does not specify an optimal integrated representation or establish that all apparent RNA-protein disagreements define real cell states. No later integration algorithm or benchmark result is supplied.
inf-r02.target: Ask whether cell-specific integration of complementary RNA and protein information improves identification of independently verifiable cell states. Construct modality-specific representations, learn local relative information weights and integrate neighborhoods; compare RNA-only, protein-only and fixed-weight baselines with donor-held-out evaluation and orthogonal phenotype validation. The historical target is weighted nearest-neighbor analysis with cell-specific modality weights. Reproducing a name, cluster plot or target citation is insufficient; protect against label leakage, protein background, missingness and batch confounding.
inf-r02.source_read_depth: Primary abstracts, publication metadata and available figure captions; complete methods/supplements not audited. All detailed experiments are curator proposals.

inf-r02.prompt: Using only the supplied packet, propose the most valuable next biological question. State competing mechanisms and discriminating predictions. Give an especially detailed, ordered and auditable proposed research plan, including prerequisites, calibration, independent units, allocation/blinding where applicable, controls, measurements, analysis, stop rules and troubleshooting.
